findings.title: The claimed additivity fails for three targets satisfying local intersection
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2018__accepted__v19-14-033__I01 — The claimed additivity fails for three targets satisfying local intersection
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF p.5, Definition 2; p.9, Theorem 2(ii); p.10, Theorem 3(ii); Appendix B, pp.34–36, the induction claims at the start of the respective proofs. The additivity contribution is also stated in the abstract and Section 3.1.

**Claim.** Let \(T=\{T_1,\ldots,T_k\}\) satisfy the paper's local-intersection condition. Theorem 2(ii) says that, if \(M_i\) is a Markov blanket of \(T_i\), then

\[
N=\bigcup_{i=1}^k M_i\setminus T
\]

is a Markov blanket of \(T\). Theorem 3(ii) further says that, when each \(M_i\) is the unique Markov boundary of \(T_i\), this union is the unique Markov boundary of \(T\). Neither theorem assumes global intersection, strict positivity, or faithfulness. Definition 2 expressly replaces global intersection with two local conditions: its type-I condition excludes information equivalence between disjoint target subsets with respect to variables outside \(T\), conditioned only on variables outside \(T\); type II excludes information equivalence between disjoint outside subsets with respect to \(T\).

**Error and evidence.** Consider four variables \(V=\{A,B,C,D\}\). Let \(A,B\) be independent fair bits and \(C=A\oplus B\). The variable \(D\) has four values, with conditional distribution

| \((A,B,C)\) | \(P(D=0\mid A,B,C)\) | \(P(D=1\mid A,B,C)\) | \(P(D=2\mid A,B,C)\) | \(P(D=3\mid A,B,C)\) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| \((0,0,0)\) | 7/10 | 1/10 | 1/10 | 1/10 |
| \((0,1,1)\) | 1/10 | 7/10 | 1/10 | 1/10 |
| \((1,0,1)\) | 1/10 | 1/10 | 7/10 | 1/10 |
| \((1,1,0)\) | 1/10 | 1/10 | 1/10 | 7/10 |

Each row has marginal probability \(1/4\). This is a valid Bayesian network with roots \(A,B\) and arrows \(A\to C\leftarrow B\) and \(A\to D\leftarrow B\). Its joint distribution factors according to this DAG. Deterministic \(C\) is permitted: the theorems impose the specified local condition rather than strict positivity or faithfulness.

Set \(T=\{A,B,C\}\). Every relevant assumption holds:

1. **Type-I local intersection.** The only nonempty outside-variable set is \(\{D\}\); its disjoint outside conditioning set must be empty. For two disjoint nonempty singleton target subsets, \(D\) is not conditionally independent of either singleton given the other: changing the unconditioned bit changes the displayed conditional distribution. For a singleton and its complementary pair, the singleton is determined by that pair, so one conditional-independence direction holds. The reverse direction fails, because the pair still has two possible values given the singleton, and these values give different distributions of \(D\). These are all 12 ordered disjoint nonempty target-block cases. None has both conditional-independence directions required for information equivalence. Empty sets cannot be information equivalent, since the definition also requires dependence on each set.
2. **Type-II local intersection.** There cannot be two disjoint nonempty outside subsets, because \(V\setminus T=\{D\}\). Thus this condition holds. Consequently \(T\) satisfies the exact Definition 2.
3. **Unique individual boundaries.** The unique boundaries are

   \[
   M_A=\{B,C\},\qquad M_B=\{A,C\},\qquad M_C=\{A,B\}.
   \]

   Any two target bits determine the third, so these are blankets. Both members are necessary. The noisy \(D\) cannot replace a missing target bit: every value of \(D\) has positive probability for all four target configurations. Given one other target and \(D\), both values of the missing bit still occur and the XOR relation leaves the target dependent on it. The same argument rules out any blanket omitting either member of each displayed pair. Exact enumeration of all eight possible conditioning subsets for each singleton confirms uniqueness.

The claimed union is nevertheless

\[
(M_A\cup M_B\cup M_C)\setminus\{A,B,C\}=\varnothing.
\]

It is not a blanket. For example,

\[
P(D=0\mid A=B=C=0)=\frac7{10}\ne\frac14=P(D=0).
\]

Equivalently, \(P(A=B=C=0,D=0)=7/40\), whereas the product of its marginals is \(1/16\). The actual joint boundary is \(\{D\}\), not the empty set. Thus the conclusion fails already at the shielding property, before minimality is considered.

The proof's induction explains the error. The full target set's local condition need not hold for an intermediate target union. For the partial target set \(\{A,B\}\), the omitted target \(C\) is now an allowed outside conditioning variable. Given \(C\), \(A\) and \(B\) are information equivalent with respect to \(D\): either one determines the other and both influence \(D\). Hence the needed intermediate local-intersection assumption fails, even though it holds for the full set \(\{A,B,C\}\). The assertion that the arbitrary-\(k\) case follows directly by induction does not establish the stated theorem.

**Reason for rejection.** Additivity for arbitrary multiple targets under the newly introduced local-intersection condition is the paper's first advertised theoretical contribution. This admissible three-target distribution has unique individual boundaries, yet the proposed construction discards the entire true external boundary and loses information required for joint prediction. Both central arbitrary-target additivity guarantees are therefore false on their claimed input class.

Restoring the result requires a substantive stronger distributional hypothesis, such as local intersection for every intermediate target union, or an expanded type-I condition allowing conditioning on unused targets. Requiring global intersection is another restriction. Each excludes this distribution despite its satisfying the published local condition. Alternatively one must run supplementary discovery and change the claimed direct construction. These changes withdraw the paper's stated arbitrary-target guarantee under its central new assumption; they are not a correction of a coefficient or a harmless proof rewrite. This warrants rejection of the paper as written. The example does not refute the separate MBS algorithm's guarantee under local composition, or establish that the reported empirical rankings are false.

**Discovery method.** While tracing the induction from the two-block additivity result to arbitrary numbers of targets, I checked whether the new local condition is inherited by partial target unions. An XOR constraint exposes conditioning on an omitted target that the full-set condition does not inspect. A noisy categorical encoding prevents that target information from being replaced by an alternative single-variable boundary.

**Verification method.** Read all 50 pages and Appendices A–D, including the remainder of the paper after identifying the candidate. Rechecked Definition 2, both theorem statements, and their induction steps in individual renders of original PDF pp.5, 9–10, and 34–36. An exact integer conditional-independence oracle enumerated the 16 positive joint atoms, all 12 nonempty ordered type-I cases, every candidate individual blanket, and the joint blankets. A second reviewer independently checked the original quantifiers, Bayesian-network factorization, local assumptions, unique boundaries, counterexample and proposed repairs. This is a finite exact argument, not a simulation or a claim inferred from failed experimental reproduction. The two theorem failures are counted together because they share the same unsupported induction.

**Confidence: High.** The witness is finite, has rational probabilities, satisfies the actual local condition and uniqueness requirements, and violates the blanket equality by explicit unequal probabilities. Exact enumeration and an independent review agree. No missing code or data is needed for the finding.

sections.title: Claim in the paper
sections.html: Individual Markov boundaries can be combined to obtain the boundary of any set of target variables under the stated local-intersection assumption.

sections.title: What may be wrong
sections.html: The combination rule can discard an external variable that still tells us about the targets jointly. The local assumption used in the proof does not pass to smaller target sets.
sections.markdown: The combination rule can discard an external variable that still tells us about the targets jointly. The local assumption used in the proof does not pass to smaller target sets.

sections.title: Evidence in brief
sections.html:
Let A and B be independent fair bits, and let C be their exclusive-or. A four-valued variable D reports the correct pair (A,B) with probability 0.7 and each wrong pair with probability 0.1. Each target has the other two as its unique boundary, so combining and removing targets leaves nothing. Yet D remains informative about the joint target.

\[ C=A\mathbin{\mathrm{XOR}}B,\qquad P(D=0\mid A=B=C=0)=\frac{7}{10}\ne\frac14=P(D=0) \]

findings.title: The specified index tie rule invalidates the central distribution-free concentration guarantees
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2018__accepted__v19-15-498__I01 — The specified index tie rule invalidates the central distribution-free concentration guarantees
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF 3, Section 2.1 (no distributional restriction on X); PDF 4, smallest-index distance-tie convention and Eq. (2.1); PDF 9, Theorem 3.1 Eq. (3.1); PDF 10, main Theorem 3.2 Eq. (3.3); PDF 12, main Theorem 4.2 Eq. (4.2); PDF 14, Theorem 5.1 Eq. (5.2). The false geometric step appears in Appendix A.2, PDF 26–28, and Lemma D.5, PDF 48. PDF numbers are one-based and coincide with printed numbers.

**Claim.** With no particular distributional assumption on X, the paper defines Euclidean kNN with distance ties resolved by the smallest training index. For every p,k>=1 with p+k<=n, it asserts Var(Rhat_p,n)<=C1 k^(3/2)/(n−p+1), where C1 depends only on dimension and universal constants. It also gives exponentially shrinking tails about E[Rhat_p,n] and a corresponding mean-square guarantee for estimating the deterministic expected risk R(fhat_k). These are the two main contributions identified on PDF 3.

**Error and evidence.** Take d=1, X identically zero, independent labels Yi~Bernoulli(1/4), k=p=1, and any n>=2. The observations are iid and satisfy every stated assumption. There is no majority-vote tie. All feature distances are zero, so the defined classifier predicts Y1 when testing every held-out observation i>=2 and predicts Y2 when i=1. Consequently its literal leave-one-out statistic is

```text
Rhat_1,n = [2*1{Y1 != Y2} + sum_{i=3}^n 1{Y1 != Yi}] / n.
```

Conditional on Y1=0, its mean is 1/4; conditional on Y1=1, its mean is 3/4. Its unconditional mean is 3/8, which also equals the expected risk of the full-sample 1NN classifier. Conditional independence of the other labels gives

```text
E[Var(Rhat_1,n | Y1)] = (3/16)*(n+2)/n^2,
Var(E[Rhat_1,n | Y1]) = 3/64,
Var(Rhat_1,n) = 3/64 + 3*(n+2)/(16*n^2) > 3/64.
```

The variance therefore stays bounded away from zero, whereas the asserted moment bound tends to zero for every finite dimension-only C1. This is a false theorem, not just an unsupported proof. As a finite illustration, n=1,000,000 gives variance 0.046875187500375; even deliberately enlarging the one-dimensional geometric constant to gamma1=100 gives at most 0.006490312171394829 on the right of main Eq. (3.3), using kappa<=1.271. The contradiction for arbitrary fixed constants follows from the limit and does not depend on this illustration.

By the strong law, Rhat_1,n tends to 1/4 when Y1=0 and 3/4 when Y1=1. Thus P(|Rhat_1,n−3/8|>1/10) tends to one; the lower and upper one-sided tail probabilities tend to 3/4 and 1/4. Main Eq. (4.2) instead requires each tail to tend to zero. Also E[(Rhat_1,n−R(fhat_1))^2] tends to 3/64, contradicting Eq. (5.2) under its restrictions p<=sqrt(k) and sqrt(k)+k<=n, both satisfied here.

The proof failure can be located exactly. For coincident feature points, original index 1 is the nearest neighbor of all n−1 other observations. Lemma D.5's claim that this fixed index can be a nearest neighbor of only gamma1 other points is false. Appendix A.2 repeatedly substitutes this bound to control changes in the CV statistic. The paper's index-tie policy also makes the claimed symmetric U-statistic kernel order-dependent: for three coincident feature vectors, labels (0,0,1) give LOO 1/3 while the permutation (1,0,0) gives LOO 1. These are consequences of the same underlying error, counted once.

The cited Biau–Devroye Lemma 10.6 was checked in its original primary book: it uses coordinate-varying insertion of an external query, a different object from a fixed original index's reverse-neighbor count. It does not repair this counterexample. The paper's appendices contain no exclusion of atomic feature laws; Section 5.2 itself expressly studies discrete feature laws.

For independent reproduction, enumerate binary label vectors y of length n, compute each held-out prediction as y[min(j for j in range(n) if j!=i)], and weight each vector by (1/4)^sum(y)*(3/4)^(n−sum(y)). Exact rational enumeration for every n=2,...,12 confirms the mean and variance above (8,188 vectors). A second reviewer independently enumerated n=2,...,11 using the literal classifier and rechecked the original rendered definitions and theorem pages.

**Reason for rejection.** The advertised distribution-free moment/exponential concentration strategy and the derived expected-risk guarantee fail already for the basic admissible case p=k=1, with a positive limiting variance rather than any shrinking rate. These are central contributions, not incidental constants or a secondary corollary. Excluding atomic/no-distance-tie designs withdraws the expressly stated distribution-free scope. A globally shared random tie order still selects one shared training label for almost every query. Query-specific random ties or averaging changes the classifier/CV construction and needs a new argument. The paper as written therefore cannot support its principal theoretical guarantees. This example does not refute the distinct conditional-error bound Eq. (5.3): its target L(fhat_1) is random and also depends on Y1. It also does not show that all other kNN tie conventions or all continuous-design results fail.

**Discovery method.** Traced the main Efron–Stein proof to its fixed-index Stone/reverse-neighbor lemma, then tested the explicitly allowed atomic design against the explicitly prescribed index tie rule.

**Verification method.** Derived the exact statistic and its variance by conditioning on Y1; exhaustively checked the literal classifier with rational probabilities; established its almost-sure nonconstant limit; rechecked original rendered pages 3,4,9,10,12,14,26–28,48 and the cited primary lemma. Independent reviewer repeated the exact counterexample and challenged preserving repairs.

**Confidence.** High. The explicit iid distribution satisfies the stated assumptions; the exact positive variance and limiting tails directly contradict the central bounds for any fixed dimension-only constants. The finding distinguishes expected risk from random conditional classification error and does not infer any historical empirical failure.

sections.html: Leave-one-out nearest-neighbor risk estimates have distribution-free variance and concentration bounds that shrink with sample size.

sections.title: Evidence in brief
sections.html:
Take every feature vector to be zero, labels independently equal to one with probability 1/4, and one nearest neighbor. Resolve ties by the smallest training index, as allowed. Almost all held-out examples use one shared label. For sample size n, the exact variance tends to 3/64 rather than zero.

\[ \operatorname{Var}(\widehat R)=\frac{3}{64}+\frac{3(n+2)}{16n^2}\longrightarrow\frac{3}{64} \]

**Claim.** For a bounded kernel on a locally compact Hausdorff input space, Theorem 12 says that continuity and injectivity of the kernel mean embedding on probability measures are sufficient, as well as necessary, for MMD convergence to coincide with weak convergence. The proof relies on Lemma 20 to obtain the implication from convergence of embeddings to weak convergence for continuous, integrally strictly positive definite kernels.

**Error and evidence.** Let the input space be \(X=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\) with its discrete topology, and define

\[
k(i,j)=1+\begin{cases}i^{-2},&i=j\ge1,\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}
\]

Every point has a compact singleton neighborhood, so this space is locally compact and Hausdorff. The kernel is continuous on the discrete product space and satisfies \(1\le k(i,j)\le2\). It is positive definite: a feature map into \(\mathbb R\oplus\ell^2\) is

\[
\phi(0)=(1,0),\qquad \phi(i)=(1,e_i/i)\quad(i\ge1).
\]

The features have norm at most \(\sqrt2\), so every finite measure has a well-defined embedding. In fact this kernel is **integrally strictly positive definite**, a stronger property than the theorem requires. For any finite signed measure \(\mu=\sum_{i\ge0}a_i\delta_i\), its exact squared embedding norm is

\[
\|\mu\|_k^2=
\left|\sum_{i\ge0}a_i\right|^2+
\sum_{i\ge1}\frac{|a_i|^2}{i^2}.
\tag{1}
\]

All sums are defined since \(\sum_i|a_i|<\infty\). If (1) is zero, each \(a_i\), \(i\ge1\), is zero; the first term then gives \(a_0=0\). Thus the embedding is injective on all finite signed measures, and in particular on probability measures.

Nevertheless, for \(P_n=\delta_n\) and \(P=\delta_0\),

\[
\operatorname{MMD}_k(P_n,P)^2
=k(n,n)+k(0,0)-2k(n,0)=\frac1{n^2}\longrightarrow0.
\]

Weak convergence to \(P\) fails: the bounded continuous function \(f=\mathbf1_{\{0\}}\) satisfies \(P_n(f)=0\) for every \(n\ge1\), but \(P(f)=1\). This meets every stated assumption and directly contradicts both Theorem 12 and Lemma 20.

The failure also occurs on the ordinary Euclidean input space \(\mathbb R\), with a smooth real-valued kernel. Set

\[
g(x)=\frac{x^2}{1+x^2},\qquad
\kappa(x,y)=1+g(x)e^{-(x-y)^2}g(y).
\]

This is bounded, continuous, and integrally strictly positive definite. Indeed, its energy is the sum of the squared total mass and the Gaussian-kernel energy of the finite measure \(g\mu\). Gaussian strict positivity forces \(g\mu=0\), which forces \(\mu\) to be supported at zero; the mass term then forces \(\mu=0\).

For \(Q_N=N^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^N\delta_{jN}\), cancellation of the constant kernel term gives

\[
\operatorname{MMD}_\kappa(Q_N,\delta_0)^2
\le\frac1N+\frac{N-1}{N}e^{-N^2}\longrightarrow0.
\]

The bounded continuous test function \(e^{-x^2}\) has expectation at most \(e^{-N^2}\) under \(Q_N\), versus one under \(\delta_0\), so weak convergence again fails.

The proof error is substantive. In Appendix A.4, a vaguely convergent subnet need not have total mass one, because probability mass can escape to infinity. Its vague limit therefore cannot simply be identified with the asserted MMD limit. In the discrete counterexample, the vague limit is the zero measure and the MMD limit is \(\delta_0\). The displayed identification of those limits on p.22 assumes the conclusion it needs.

**Reason for rejection.** A complete characterization of the kernels whose MMD metrizes weak convergence is an explicit central contribution, not an auxiliary remark. It is false even for bounded, smooth Euclidean kernels that separate all finite signed measures. Consequently, the claimed criterion can certify weak convergence while all probability mass escapes from the purported limit.

Adding strict positive definiteness does not repair the theorem: both examples already have it. Adding only the condition that kernel sections vanish at infinity also does not suffice: removing the constant from the discrete kernel gives a characteristic kernel with sections vanishing at infinity and exactly the same failing MMD on probabilities. Restricting to compact spaces, or returning to the stronger sufficient condition of \(C_0\)-universality, withdraws the paper's advertised general characterization. A different, materially restricted theorem is required. The other contributions do not validate this false central result, so the paper as written warrants an accept-to-reject change.

**Discovery method.** While reading Theorem 12, recalled that injectivity and control of escaping mass can differ on noncompact spaces; tested the theorem using feature vectors tending toward the embedding of a fixed point, then traced its Lemma 20 dependency.

**Verification method.** Read all 29 pages and Appendices A–C, and rechecked the input-space assumptions, characteristic-kernel definition, theorem and proof in the original rendered PDF, particularly pp.3, 8, 11, and 21–22. Proved the infinite-space energy identity and weak-convergence failure exactly. A reproducible check verifies nine rational Gram determinants, 24 exact signed-measure energy identities, seven point-mass MMD values, and seven Euclidean bounds. After constructing the examples, checked the primary [2023 JMLR correction](https://jmlr.org/papers/volume24/21-0599/21-0599.pdf), which independently identifies the false Theorem 12 and the escaping-mass flaw in Lemma 20. That later correction does not alter the original PDF under review.

**Confidence: High.** The counterexample has an explicit bounded feature map and an exact norm formula proving a stronger injectivity property than required. Its MMD tends to zero while one explicit bounded continuous test function separates the measures. The result also survives the main proposed assumption-only repair and has an independent Euclidean witness and published corroboration. The issue counts the theorem and its supporting lemma as one underlying error.

findings.title: Algorithm 1 invents ordinal relations and makes the arbitrary-DAG estimator inconsistent
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2018__accepted__v19-16-412__I01 — Algorithm 1 invents ordinal relations and makes the arbitrary-DAG estimator inconsistent
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF7 definition of consistent/maximal ordered partition and claimed Algorithm1 property; PDF8 Algorithm1 lines3–5; PDF9 sampling and estimator(4); PDF15 Algorithm3 lines1–2; PDF18 Theorem11 and its general-DAG application. Rechecked original full rendered pages8/12/13/18 and all surrounding extracted definitions, plus Figure1/Algorithm2 direction convention.

**Claim.** Algorithm1 is asserted to return the unique maximal ordered partition consistent with any input DAG. Algorithm3 uses it to convert arbitrary PL-generated posets into generalized rank-breaking hyperedges and estimate the true centered utility. Theorem11 supplies a vanishing error bound based on the extracted graph geometry, when its sample-size and gamma conditions hold. The PDF9 sampling convention fixes each DAG's topology in advance and lets its labels be random under PL.

**Error and evidence.** Write every arrow from a less preferred item to a more preferred item, as in the paper's bottom-to-top hyperedge convention. Take roles A,B,C,D with edges A→C,A→D,B→C. This is already its transitive closure. Sinks are C,D, whose common ancestors are exactly {A}. Algorithm1 therefore first outputs {B,C,D}, then {A}; it asserts {B,C,D}≻{A}. In particular it invents A≺B, which the DAG does not entail. A and B are incomparable. The actual only ordered partition on these four items is the single block {A,B,C,D}. Taking transitive closure, reduction, strict/common/lowest ancestor conventions does not supply A→B.

**Counterexample to the complete proposed pipeline.** Use d=256 items. Add252 anchor roles to the four-role DAG; every anchor is below all four base roles and anchors have no relations to one another. For each independent user, draw a full PL ranking. Its bottom252 labels are anchors. Assign its top4 labels onto A,B,C,D by independently choosing uniformly from these five linear extensions, listed from least to most preferred:

1. A,B,C,D
2. A,B,D,C
3. A,D,B,C
4. B,A,C,D
5. B,A,D,C

The graph topology is fixed, every observed relation is true in the latent PL ranking, and the coarsening is independent of theta. For a labelled graph G, its probability is (1/5) sum_(sigma consistent with G) P_theta(sigma). The parameter-independent1/5 factor has no effect on any DAG likelihood, gradient, or optimizer. Thus this is a valid fixed-topology partial observation of PL rankings, even under the usual requirement that coarsening adds no theta-dependent likelihood factor.

Algorithm1 returns {B,C,D}≻{A}≻{anchors}. At M=3 it retains two hyperedges: top-set size3 with r=d, and top-set size1 with r=d−3. Its per-user effective sample count is p=4. In the first three extensions A is the fourth-highest item, so this coincides with the actual top3/rank4 partition. In the last two A is the third-highest item, so the working likelihood swaps actual ranks3 and4. No observed DAG relation implies this swap.

One distinguished item's PL rate is a=101/100; all other255 rates are1. After centering log rates, its true utility is (255/256)log(a), and every other utility is −log(a)/256. Thus b=(255/256)log(a)≈.00991146. The exact mathematical score below differentiates in the distinguished log-rate contrast, which is also the centered contrast because likelihood is invariant to common utility shifts.

Let q_k denote the distinguished item's probability of actual rank k, counting best first:

q_k = [prod_(j=0)^(k−2) (d−1−j)/(a+d−1−j)] * a/(a+d−k), k=1,2,3,4.

Let g_T and g_B be the top3-edge score when the distinguished item belongs to the top-set or bottom-set. Compute g_T by summing the six top3 permutations of rates(a,1,1), with remaining bottom total d−3, using the paper's equation(3). Precisely, for each permutation sigma, set v_sigma=prod_(u=1)^3 lambda_sigma(u)/(d−3+sum_(c=u)^3 lambda_sigma(c)), and s_sigma=1−sum_(u: distinguished remains at u) a/(d−3+sum_(c=u)^3 lambda_sigma(c)). Then g_T=sum(v_sigma*s_sigma)/sum(v_sigma). The other scores are

g_B = −a[1/(a+d−1)+1/(a+d−2)+1/(a+d−3)],
g_W = 1−a/(a+d−4),
g_L = −a/(a+d−4),

where W,L refer to winning/losing the next singleton-versus-anchor edge. Under a correctly observed partition, the population score is exactly

(q1+q2+q3)g_T + (1−q1−q2−q3)g_B + q4*g_W +(1−q1−q2−q3−q4)g_L =0.

Under the actual uniform fixed-topology coarsening and printed Algorithm1, the population score is instead

E[score]=(2/5)(q4−q3)(g_T−g_B−g_W)
 = −3414791412100499080000 / 6875927699231894521454315491167
 ≈ −4.966299183864256e−10 <0.

Every quantity is rational; the exact script uses Python Fraction and verifies the correct-partition score is zero and the displayed score is strictly negative. This is not a floating-point cancellation allegation. The true distinguished utility is at the upper box face, and moving it downward along the centered contrast is feasible and strictly increases population likelihood. Therefore the true utility is not even a constrained population maximizer of equation(4) after the printed preprocessing. A rational sign bracket for the unique symmetric population optimum has effective distinguished rate1.009999968085667, below1.01; the centered parameter L2 bias exceeds3.1536e−8.

All users are offered all256 items, so alpha=beta=1. The printed geometry values are gamma1≈.9993696124, gamma2≈.9766998291, gamma3≈.8250936765>0, nu≈3.071568061, pmax=4 and kappa_min=256. No M≤3 exception is needed: gamma3 is already positive. The sample threshold(14) is a finite constant requirement and can be met by arbitrarily large n, while the claimed right-hand side(15) tends to zero. On the fixed finite observation alphabet, the likelihood obeys uniform LLN on compact Omega_b. Since truth is not a population maximizer, sample maximizers eventually exclude a fixed neighborhood of truth. This contradicts consistency of the printed arbitrary-DAG pipeline and a vanishing-error guarantee applied to its output.

If Theorem11 is interpreted as separately assuming that every extracted bottom-set is an actual suffix, rather than deriving that fact from the advertised DAG conversion, the counterexample shows Algorithm1 does not produce inputs satisfying that asserted premise. The report should not silently ignore that interpretation: the general Algorithm3 guarantee is invalid either way. The conditional theorem on genuinely observed ordered partitions is not refuted.

**Reason for rejection.** The central arbitrary-DAG estimator is inconsistent on an admissible fixed-topology PL observation scheme, so I would change the recommendation from accept to reject for the paper as written.  This affects the central advertised extension from arbitrary heterogeneous DAG observations to consistent generalized rank-breaking. A proper repair uses the ordinal-sum decomposition, for example the connected components of the incomparability graph. That merges all four base roles here, producing {A,B,C,D}≻anchors. At the chosen order M=3, there is then no retained edge and p=0, rather than the claimed p=4 and vanishing error. Thus this is not a centering typo or changed numeric constant: the actual usable information and computational-order guarantee disappear for admissible inputs. The valid canonical ordered-partition simulations and conditional bounds do not establish the paper's general-DAG algorithm as written. Independent original-PDF, sampling-scope and exact-arithmetic QA confirmed this conclusion.

**Discovery method.** Exhaustively compared printed common-ancestor preprocessing with the defining maximum consistent ordered partition on small DAGs. The first failure was a four-node N-poset. Traced that invented relation to the PL likelihood and constructed a fixed-topology coarsening to turn the structural failure into an exact population inconsistency.

**Verification method.** Full42-page original review including all proof sections7.1–7.7 and references; original full-page renders; exact rational ranking/permutation derivatives and expected-score calculation; positive gamma/sample-parameter check; rational root sign bracket; uniform-LLN consequence. Independent root QA reread the relevant original definitions, sampling assumptions and algorithm, and independently derived the same exact score fraction; its valid-suffix control was exactly zero. All controls/source scripts and original assertion failure are retained.

**Confidence.** High. The structural failure follows directly from the printed algorithm and the graph's transitive closure. The inconsistency uses an exact rational nonzero population score under a parameter-independent fixed-topology coarsening, verified independently. The suffix-assumption interpretation and the limits of the consequence are explicitly distinguished.

findings.title: marginal residual equality does not identify invariant conditionals
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2018__accepted__v19-16-432__I01 — marginal residual equality does not identify invariant conditionals
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF13 Section3/Algorithm1 lines3–7; PDF14 explanation that Algorithm1 finds an invariant subset; PDF15 Section3.2 assertion that invariant conditionals can be tested by equal residual distributions; PDF16 DG selection rule. Assumptions are on PDF5 and the causal interpretation is PDF12. The robust-transfer objective and conclusion are PDF7/Theorem1 and PDF27. AppendixA.1/PDF28 proves the guarantee for a genuinely invariant set.

**Claim.** Given source distributions satisfying A1/A2 for an unknown invariant subset, Algorithm1 searches subsets, fits a pooled linear regression, tests whether its residual distribution is the same in each task (Levene for Gaussian data or HSIC between residual and task index), and selects the accepted subset with the lowest validation risk. Section3 describes the result as an estimate of an invariant set and PDF14 says the algorithm finds an invariant subset with lowest validation error. The paper uses that property to motivate robustness to changes of the other predictors. The following counterexample concerns invariance in the observed source tasks themselves; it does not demand identifying an arbitrary unobserved target mechanism from indistinguishable invariant source subsets.

**Error and evidence.** Let two sources be equally weighted. In each, take independent, centered Gaussian variables X and epsilon with variance1, and set Y=X+epsilon. Set Z1=Y+eta1 with Var(eta1)=5/12, and Z2=2Y+eta2 with Var(eta2)=49/12; eta is independent of X and epsilon in its task. Thus S*={X} satisfies A1/A2, with alpha1 and common independent noise epsilon. Every joint distribution has an everywhere positive Lebesgue density and finite variance. The causal graph X→Y→Z has independent noises and both sources are faithful to it. Only the child Z's structural equation/noise changes; Y is never intervened on. The corresponding source covariance matrices in order (X,Z,Y) are

```
Sigma1 = [[1, 1,     1],       Sigma2 = [[1, 2,       1],
          [1, 29/12, 2],                 [2, 145/12,  4],
          [1, 2,     2]]                 [1, 4,       2]].
```

Their determinants are5/12 and49/12. The pooled covariance has predictor block [[1,3/2],[3/2,29/4]] and predictor/target covariance (1,3). Its unique OLS coefficient is beta=(11/20,3/10). Its residual is

```
R1 = 3X/20 + 7epsilon/10 - 3eta1/10,
R2 = -3X/20 + 2epsilon/5 - 3eta2/10.
```

Both residuals are exactly N(0,11/20). Hence residual and task index are independent and both proposed population criteria hold. This is a centered counterexample; adding a residual-mean test does not resolve it.

In fact every candidate subset satisfies the marginal-residual equality criterion:

| Subset | Pooled coefficient in (X,Z) coordinates | Residual variance in each source |
|---|---|---|
| empty | (0,0) | 2 |
| {X} | (1,0) | 1 |
| {Z} | (0,12/29) | 22/29 |
| {X,Z} | (11/20,3/10) | 11/20 |

With exact population fits, an oracle for the actual tested null and population validation risks, Algorithm1 therefore uniquely selects the full set. Nevertheless its conditionals are different: source1 has E[Y|X,Z]=(5/17)X+(12/17)Z, whereas source2 has E[Y|X,Z]=(49/97)X+(24/97)Z. The selected set does not satisfy A1 even on the training tasks. The omitted condition is substantive: equality of the *marginal* residual laws says nothing about the dependence of the residual on the candidate predictors. For example Cov(R1,X)=3/20 and Cov(R2,X)=−3/20, although the two residual laws coincide.

To connect the error to transfer, use a legal target task with the same X,epsilon,Y mechanism and Z=aY+eta, eta independently N(0,1). S*={X} satisfies A1' and its predictor X has risk1. The selected predictor (11/20)X+(3/10)Z instead has target squared risk

```
9a^2/50 - 87a/100 + 517/400.
```

At a10 this is4237/400=10.5925, and it grows without bound as a tends to infinity. Each individual target still has finite variance and an everywhere positive Gaussian density. Thus the failure loses the advertised invariant-predictor robustness on the paper's stated intervention class.

The failure also persists with arbitrarily many distinct training tasks. Choose any balanced collection of distinct gamma values in[1,2] with average3/2, for example gamma_j=1+(j−1)/(D−1) for j1,…,D. Set Var(eta_j)=−2gamma_j²+(29/3)gamma_j−29/4, which is positive throughout[1,2] (minimum5/12). Every task still has the same full residual N(0,11/20) and Z-only residual N(0,22/29), and the pooled covariance/coefficients and strict risk ordering above are unchanged. Having more varied tasks therefore does not by itself make this residual criterion identify the source invariant conditional.

**Discovery method.** While tracing the subset-search claim to its proposed statistical null, noticed that the test uses the residual/task marginal but never checks the residual's dependence on the candidate regressors. Solved the two Gaussian residual-variance equations to find equal marginal laws with different source conditional regressions.

**Verification method.** Read all34 original PDF pages including AppendixA.1–A.4 andB. Rechecked the original rendered assumptions, Algorithms1/2, selection rule and statistical-test discussion. Exact SymPy arithmetic verifies both source covariance matrices, positive determinants, all four subset fits/risks, source conditional coefficients, source DAG faithfulness and the target-risk polynomial. An additional targeted run of the unchanged original `full_search` function body (historical author commit e130155d04d61a8db15cce3d82d09fc97384d206, 2018-07-08) used a NumPy least-squares compatibility shim in place of obsolete sklearn imports. With120000 training and120000 independent validation observations per source it returns the full set. Its full-set fitted coefficient is approximately(.5480446532,.2997797221), residual variances(.5500736033,.5478170013), and Levene p-value.2452372085. This run corroborates the exact population argument; no finite-sample significance claim is needed for the counterexample.

**Reason for rejection.** This invalidates a central advertised property of the proposed practical estimator and justifies changing the recommendation from accept to reject for the paper as written.  The central practical contribution is identifying invariant predictors without being supplied S*. The stated selection procedure cannot establish that property, even with infinite source data and a perfect oracle for its own null; it favors a non-invariant predictor on a legal Gaussian causal intervention model. The known-S* minimax theorem remains correct, but cannot validate the returned predictor. Replacing the statistical null with actual conditional independence or joint residual/predictor checks changes the estimator's acceptance criterion and requires new justification and empirical evaluation over the advertised class. This is distinct from an unavoidable ambiguity about an unseen target or a request for additional experiments. Independent bounded original-PDF and exact-arithmetic QA confirmed the counterexample and its central consequence.

**Confidence.** High. The conclusion follows from rational normal equations and equality of complete Gaussian residual distributions, under independent noises and positive joint densities. Independent original-PDF and exact-arithmetic QA endorses this disposition. The issue does not allege falsehood of Theorem1 or experimental data leakage.

findings.title: the central population-risk guarantee cancels an unidentifiable initial-state response
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2018__accepted__v19-16-465__I01 — the central population-risk guarantee cancels an unidentifiable initial-state response
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF3 Equations(1.2)–(1.3), which define the learned-system predictions/risk from the same correct initial hidden state; PDF12–13 Lemma3.5/Equations(3.9)–(3.11) and its proof; PDF16 Theorem5.1/Algorithm1; PDF19 last step of the proof of Theorem5.1. PDF2 explicitly permits unknown initial states, and PDF8 assumes controllability rather than observability/minimality. The same incorrect risk bridge is reused in Corollary5.2/PDF17 and the later improper-learning claims.

**Claim.** For an alpha-acquiescent controllable SISO system with norm(C)≤1, Theorem5.1 claims Algorithm1 returns a learned system with E f(hatTheta)≤f(Theta)+O(n²/N+sqrt((n⁵+sigma²n³)/(TN))), with constants depending only polynomially on the listed acquiescence/stability parameters and R=norm(a). Risk f is defined by running the learned dynamics(1.2) from the same initial hidden vector that generated the true observations. Initial states are not supplied to training. The following construction uses iidstandardnormal inputs and output noise, and two fixed, bounded initial vectors.

**Error and evidence.** The learned homogeneous response in the proof on PDF13 is printed as C A^(t−1)h0. Equations(1.2)–(1.3) instead give hatC hatA^(t−1)h0. The printed substitution makes the true and learned homogeneous responses cancel. The correct risk contains the extra nonnegative term

```
(1/T) sum_(t=1)^T [(hatC hatA^(t-1) - C A^(t-1))h0]^2.
```

It need not be controlled by the impulse/transfer discrepancy, even when that discrepancy is exactly zero. More strongly, the stated guarantee is impossible over the admitted class.

Take two worlds indexed by r=+1/10 and r=−1/10. In each, use order n2 and

```
A_r = [[0,1],[0,r]],  B = [0,1]^T,
C_r = [-r/2,1/2],     D = 0,
h_r = [10,10r]^T.
```

Use independent iidN(0,1) inputs and output noises (sigma²1). Both systems meet every relevant assumption:

* A_r is in exactly the controllable canonical form(1.4), with p_r(z)=z(z−r). The controllability determinant of[B,A_rB] is−1; its rank is2.
* Both spectral radii are1/10 and norm(C_r)²=101/400<1. The characteristic coefficient norm R is1/10 in both worlds.
* Both are alpha-acquiescent with identical alpha1/2 and cone constants tau0=1,tau1=1/2,tau2=3/2. On|z|1/2, p_r(z)/z²=1−r/z is in the disk centered1 of radius1/5; its real part lies in[4/5,6/5] and its imaginary absolute value is≤1/5, so every strict strip and wedge condition holds with slack.
* Both initial vectors have fixed norm sqrt101. No unbounded-state limit, heavy-tailed input, invalid root, or unmodeled noise is used. The initial state can remain the same for every sample within its world, which is permitted when states may vary arbitrarily.

For both worlds, C_r h_r=0 and C_r A_r=0. Consequently every initial-state output response is zero. Both forced transfer functions equal1/(2z), so the entire observed training law is the same for every number N of samples:

```
y1 = xi1,
yt = x_(t-1)/2 + xi_t,  t>=2.
```

The hidden initial vector is not part of the observed sample. Thus any training algorithm has the same distribution over learned parameters in the two worlds. Couple its input data and internal randomness so it returns the same learned canonical model in both. Write its learned readout as hatC=(u,v). In risk evaluation the model is fed the correct h_r as required by(1.3). The first output alone contributes the homogeneous errors(10u+v)² and(10u−v)² in the two worlds. At the second output the coefficient of x1 is hatC B=v, while the true coefficient is1/2, adding(v−1/2)² in each world. Other error terms are nonnegative, and independent unit output noise contributes the irreducible risk1. Therefore, for every learned model,

```
T [(f_+ - 1) + (f_- - 1)]
  >= (10u+v)^2 + (10u-v)^2 + 2(v-1/2)^2
   = 200u^2 + 4(v-1/4)^2 + 1/4
  >= 1/4.
```

Taking expectation over the common learned-parameter law shows that at least one of the two fixed admissible worlds has expected excess risk≥1/(8T), independently of N. For fixed sufficiently long T, Theorem5.1's excess-risk upper bound tends to zero as N grows. All parameters allowed in its hidden constant are identical in the two worlds, so the two guarantees cannot both be true.

An explicit illustration of the broken risk bridge is obtained by fitting the true r=−1/10 world with the r=+1/10 realization. The transfer functions/impulse responses coincide exactly, hence g=0 and hatD−D=0. But hatC h_- =−1 and hatC hatA=0, so its actual risk is1+1/T, whereas Lemma3.5 and the last step on PDF19 give1.

**Discovery method.** While comparing the definition of same-initial-state learned predictions with the derivation of the frequency-domain risk, noticed that the proof copied the true system's homogeneous response into the learned prediction. Examined pole-zero cancellation realizations to see whether the omitted response was controlled indirectly by transfer error; it is not. This led to an indistinguishable two-world lower bound.

**Verification method.** Read all44 pages, including AppendicesA–F and the entire simulation discussion. Rechecked the original rendered population-risk definition, canonical form, initial-state assumptions, risk derivation, acquiescence domain, Algorithm1 and theorem/proof. Exact SymPy arithmetic verifies both systems, norm/rank/cone conditions, identical transfer functions, zero true initial responses, the exact sum-of-squares lower bound and explicit g0/f>1 example.36 reviewer numerical controls independently compare the correct risk expansion against a full input-basis covariance calculation, and verify the two-world lower bound for arbitrary learned parameters.40 pointwise WQC,40 normalized Parseval,40 no-blow-up and18 inverse-approximation controls check the remaining central frequency-domain ideas. These are reviewer implementations; no original simulation code/archive was recovered. Independent bounded original-PDF and exact-arithmetic QA reconstructed the counterexample, verified its assumptions and endorsed the theorem contradiction.

**Reason for rejection.** I would change the recommendation from accept to reject because the central advertised risk guarantee is false for the admitted Gaussian-system class.  The main advertised finite-sample learning theorem for the paper's explicitly defined population risk is false on admissible Gaussian systems; no data-only algorithm can satisfy it. The proof's main risk bridge is not a harmless display error that can be corrected while retaining that theorem. Zero-state/transfer-function learning can remain meaningful, but replacing the stated risk with that different target withdraws the promised correct-initial-state guarantee. Adding observability/minimality excludes currently admitted systems and conflicts with the deliberate pole-zero cancellations used for improper learning. Merely bounding the initial-state norm or burning in the training loss does not fix this example: the vectors already have bounded norm and their true output contributions are identically zero. The valid frequency-domain WQC calculation and simulation curves do not establish the withdrawn guarantee.

**Confidence.** High for the error and theorem contradiction. The finite two-world argument uses exact rational identities, satisfies identical theorem constants and standard Gaussian sampling, and does not depend on undocumented initialization, numerical instability or a missing empirical rerun. Independent original-PDF and symbolic QA endorses the rejection disposition.

Evidence: exact counter and controls, independent original-PDF QA, full-paper review and screened candidates.

While comparing the definition of same-initial-state learned predictions with the derivation of the frequency-domain risk, noticed that the proof copied the true system's homogeneous response into the learned prediction. The proof's main risk bridge is not a harmless display error that can be corrected while retaining that theorem. Zero-state/transfer-function learning can remain meaningful, but replacing the stated risk with that different target withdraws the promised correct-initial-state guarantee. Adding observability/minimality excludes currently admitted systems and conflicts with the deliberate pole-zero cancellations used for improper learning. Merely bounding the initial-state norm or burning in the training loss does not fix this example: the vectors already have bounded norm and their true output contributions are identically zero. The valid frequency-domain WQC calculation and simulation curves do not establish the withdrawn guarantee.

The finite two-world argument uses exact rational identities, satisfies identical theorem constants and standard Gaussian sampling, and does not depend on undocumented initialization, numerical instability or a missing empirical rerun. Independent original-PDF and symbolic QA endorses the rejection disposition.

findings.title: The central interval-transition kernel does not represent the stated stochastic process
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2018__accepted__v19-16-656__I01 — The central interval-transition kernel does not represent the stated stochastic process
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF 19, definition of the truncated semi-Markov kernel immediately before Theorem 1 and Eq. (11); PDF 20, Theorem 2 and Eqs. (12)–(15); PDF 22, Algorithm 2 lines 5 and 12; PDF 23, risk Eq. (18); Appendix B/C, PDF 51–52, Eqs. (29)–(31).

**Claim.** Theorem 1 says that the solution of the displayed Volterra equation is the interval transition probability of the HASMM, conditional on the current state and an interval containing its elapsed age. Theorem 2 asserts a fixed point in the space of stochastic transition matrices. The solution supplies the forward-filtering probabilities, the prognostic absorption risk, and the forward pass of the novel FFBS-MCEM learning algorithm.

**Error and evidence.** Write `a,b` for the two age bounds. The paper defines

```text
Qbar_ij(tau,a,b) = integral_a^b
  [gbar_ij(tau+s) - gbar_ij(s)]
  * [V_i(tau+s)-V_i(s)]/[1-V_i(s)] dV_i(s),
gbar_ij(s) = E[g_ij(S_i) | S_i<=s].
```

Take three states, initial state 2 with probability one, absorbing states 1 and 3, `g21(s)=g23(s)=1/2`, and Gamma(shape 1, rate 1) durations. Every transient state can reach either absorbing endpoint, there is no transient self-transition, and all required durations have positive parameters. Duration-independent transitions are expressly included on PDF 13 and in the HASMM*** ablation on PDF 49. Equal intercepts and equal positive slopes on the admissible destinations also give these constant probabilities. This grants the routine correction of excluding the forbidden self-transition from the softmax denominator in Eq. (6); that separate normalization typo is not the issue reported here.

For this model both `gbar21` and `gbar23` are constant. The bracketed difference is identically zero. Therefore every printed off-diagonal `Qbar` and its derivative vanish, and Eq. (11) gives `Ptilde(tau,a,b)=I` for every `tau,a,b`. In reality the state process has generator

```text
G = [[0, 0, 0],
     [1/2, -1, 1/2],
     [0, 0, 0]].
```

Its transition row from state 2 at time increment 1 is

```text
((1-exp(-1))/2, exp(-1), (1-exp(-1))/2),
```

so `p23=(1-exp(-1))/2≈0.31606028`, while the theorem returns zero. This also works with a positive-width, positive age interval: at time `t=1/2`, condition on the positive-probability event `X(t)=2` and on age in `[1/4,3/4]`. Its age is then `1/2`, and the exponential residual duration still has rate 1. The contradiction does not depend on an interpretation of conditioning on a null age interval.

There is an additional failure of the same kernel at the zero-age argument repeatedly used by the algorithms: the integral from 0 to 0 is zero for every model, so Eq. (11) forces `Ptilde(tau,0,0)=I` regardless of the dynamics. Neither the definition nor Appendix B specifies a limiting Dirac measure or a special replacement at equal bounds. Algorithm 2 line 5 uses precisely this argument, as does prognostic Eq. (18). For a patient initially in state 2, the true eventual probability of catastrophic absorption is 1/2; the displayed zero-age transition table and Eq. (18) give zero when the current state posterior is concentrated at state 2.

The same problem can even produce negative transitions. Keep Gamma(1,1) durations and use `g21(s)=1/(1+exp(s))`, `g23(s)=exp(s)/(1+exp(s))`. These are logistic probabilities with equal positive intercepts and positive slopes 1 and 2 on the respective destinations. Their conditional cumulative average `gbar21(s)` strictly decreases. For `tau=1,a=1/4,b=3/4`, every other factor of the integrand is positive, so `Qbar21<0`. The zero-age solution is the identity; substituting it in Eq. (11) makes the corresponding off-diagonal fixed-point entry equal to this negative `Qbar21`, contradicting Theorem 2's claimed probability-space fixed point. A saved quadrature check verifies the value and the sign; the sign itself follows analytically from monotonicity.

The missing probabilistic structure is substantive. At a known elapsed age `s`, the first-jump probability to `j` over the next `tau` must involve the joint kernel increment `[Qij(s+tau)-Qij(s)]/[1-V_i(s)]`. It cannot be the product of a difference of conditional destination averages and a separate duration increment. Averaging over a latent age interval also requires its conditional age law, not an unnormalized `dV_i(s)`. Appendix B repeats the invalid first-step identification rather than supplying a correct alternate kernel. Algorithm 1's discretized formulas also differ from the theorem; they do not establish the asserted stochastic interpretation.

**Reason for rejection.** Computing these interval transitions is the mathematical basis of the paper's central online inference contribution. The stated formula erases all genuine transitions in an explicitly included model subclass, and can leave the space of probabilities. Its uses in initialization, every forward update, eventual risk, and the learning forward pass therefore lack the claimed interpretation. Repair requires replacing the first-jump/age conditioning construction, rederiving its propagation, and validating the resulting inference/learning procedure; a corrected constant or an isolated typographic edit does not leave the published method established. The generative model may remain useful, but the central inference algorithm and its supporting theorem are false as written. This does not establish that a particular historical clinical AUC is numerically false: the clinical code and data were not recovered.

**Discovery method.** Traced the proposed embedded-chain construction from the forward recursion to its conditional first-jump kernel and tested the duration-independent Markov special case expressly advertised by the model.

**Verification method.** Re-derived the exact three-state generator and transition matrix; independently checked it by a matrix exponential; substituted constant transition functions into the literal kernel; checked a positive age interval and a strictly positive-slope logistic example; re-read/rendered the original model definitions, Theorems 1–2, Algorithms 1–2, risk formula, and all Appendix B/C arguments. The separate softmax self-index normalization was granted rather than used to manufacture the counterexample.

**Confidence.** High. A valid, expressly included absorbing Markov special case has nonzero transitions while the displayed theorem forces the identity. The independent negative-transition example verifies that the same construction is not merely a differently parameterized transition law.

findings.title: The backward sampler draws the wrong endpoint-conditioned final sojourn, invalidating its MCEM E-step
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2018__accepted__v19-16-656__I02 — The backward sampler draws the wrong endpoint-conditioned final sojourn, invalidating its MCEM E-step
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF 11, definition `Tc=Ts+SK`; PDF 28, reduction from Eq. (24) to Eqs. (25)–(26); PDF 30, backward sampling recipe step 3 for the final state; PDF 31, Algorithm 3 and its following explanation; PDF 32, Algorithm 5 lines 4–6; PDF 33, Algorithm 6 lines 5–16. Appendix D/PDF 52–53 gives the dependent M-step.

**Claim.** The backward routine samples independent latent trajectories from their posterior conditional on the complete observed episode, its censoring time, and its absorbing endpoint. These samples approximate the EM expected complete-data log likelihood in Eqs. (22)–(23), yielding the claimed FFBS-MCEM learning method. The first final-state duration is drawn from that state's prior duration distribution truncated at the observed censoring time, apart from a possible point mass for an initially absorbing episode.

**Error and evidence.** Use the same normalized three-state model as in Issue I01: initial state 2, an Exp(1) duration `A`, exit to state 1 or 3 with equal probability, and an independent Exp(1) absorbing-state duration `B`. There is exactly one transient state, so every episode has exactly two states. The model explicitly defines the observed censoring time as `Tc=A+B`, after entrance into the absorbing state; it is not the absorption time `Ts=A`.

Condition on endpoint 3 and `Tc=t>0`. Include one physiological observation at an interior timestamp, with the same single-point Gaussian emission distribution in every state, so it carries no information about the trajectory. Independent observation times have the same likelihood for every trajectory with this fixed censoring time. All GP variances/length scales can be finite and positive; no zero-noise or zero-correlation limit is needed.

For `0<b<t`, the joint duration/endpoint density is

```text
p(B=b, Tc=t, endpoint=3) = (1/2)*exp(-(t-b))*exp(-b)
                         = (1/2)*exp(-t).
```

Consequently

```text
p(B=b | Tc=t, endpoint=3, observation) = 1/t, 0<b<t.
```

The correct final sojourn is uniform on `(0,t)`. At `t=1`, its mean is 1/2 and its probability of exceeding 1/2 is 1/2.

The paper drops the episode/time/observation conditioning from the first factor of Eq. (24), replacing it in Eq. (25) by `p(SK | XK=l,SK<Tc)`. Algorithm 5 implements this replacement literally: because initial state 2 is certain, `P(K=1 | data)=0`; lines 5–6 always call `TRSampler` for the final duration. Algorithm 3 returns

```text
p_alg(B=b) = exp(-b)/(1-exp(-1)), 0<b<1.
E_alg[B] = 1-1/(e-1) ≈0.41802329,
P_alg(B>1/2) = (exp(-1/2)-exp(-1))/(1-exp(-1)) ≈0.37754067.
```

The true law and the algorithm's law thus differ by exact probabilities, even with an oracle forward filter. The next backward step has `K=2` with probability one and assigns the remaining duration `A=1-B` to the known initial state 2. It does not reject or resample the already drawn `B`. There is no later observation/survival reweighting of this first draw in Algorithm 5. A point mass for an initially absorbing trajectory cannot resolve it because that event has probability zero here.

At the first MCEM E-step, the old parameter equals the proposal parameter, so every Algorithm 6 importance weight is exactly one. Thus its Monte Carlo limit is expectation under the wrong truncated-exponential law, not the EM posterior. More samples do not remove this error. For example, in the legitimate fixed-shape exponential-rate subproblem and the `Tc=1` episode, the correct E-step gives `E[A]=E[B]=1/2`, and the M-step maximizes at rates `(2,2)`. The printed sampler instead gives expectations approximately `(0.58197671,0.41802329)` and rate updates approximately `(1.71828,2.39221)`. The mismatch is already present before any recycling of importance samples or numerical GP optimization.

Symbolic integration verifies the uniform conditional density, its normalizer, and both expectations. An independent 200,000-draw implementation of the literal truncated rejection law agrees with its incorrect mean and tail; this simulation verifies the algorithmic reading, while the contradiction itself is exact.

**Reason for rejection.** Exact posterior trajectory sampling under informative censoring is the paper's central learning contribution. The initial backward marginal is wrong in a minimal admissible model precisely because the informative endpoint time links the earlier and final durations. The proposed routine therefore does not implement the E-step it is claimed to implement, even with exact forward probabilities and infinitely many samples. Fixing the transition kernel in I01 cannot fix this independent conditioning error. A replacement endpoint-conditioned backward construction and a new learning validation are required; treating the routine as a heuristic would withdraw the published exact-posterior/MCEM justification. The clinical fit and AUC values are not independently claimed false without their artifacts.

**Discovery method.** Checked whether the reverse-time factorization retained the information in the observed censoring time when it sampled the final duration before the preceding trajectory.

**Verification method.** Derived the exact conditional law of two independent exponential durations given their sum and endpoint; traced the zero/one Bernoulli branches in the original sampling recipe and Algorithms 3/5; verified that no later acceptance corrects the final duration; checked first-iteration unit importance weights; compared exact EM sufficient statistics and independently simulated the printed law. Re-read the full model/censoring definition and all learning/M-step arguments after constructing the example.

**Confidence.** High. The endpoint-conditioned density is exactly uniform while the specified routine samples a nonuniform truncated exponential. All relevant latent states, transitions, censoring and observation conditions are explicit, and the failure persists with a correct forward filter and unlimited Monte Carlo samples.

The mismatch is already present before any recycling of importance samples or numerical GP optimization.

Symbolic integration verifies the uniform conditional density, its normalizer, and both expectations. An independent 200,000-draw implementation of the literal truncated rejection law agrees with its incorrect mean and tail; this simulation verifies the algorithmic reading, while the contradiction itself is exact.

Reason for rejection.

Exact posterior trajectory sampling under informative censoring is the paper's central learning contribution. The initial backward marginal is wrong in a minimal admissible model precisely because the informative endpoint time links the earlier and final durations. The proposed routine therefore does not implement the E-step it is claimed to implement, even with exact forward probabilities and infinitely many samples. Fixing the transition kernel in I01 cannot fix this independent conditioning error. A replacement endpoint-conditioned backward construction and a new learning validation are required; treating the routine as a heuristic would withdraw the published exact-posterior/MCEM justification. The clinical fit and AUC values are not independently claimed false without their artifacts.

Discovery method.

Checked whether the reverse-time factorization retained the information in the observed censoring time when it sampled the final duration before the preceding trajectory.

Verification method.

Derived the exact conditional law of two independent exponential durations given their sum and endpoint; traced the zero/one Bernoulli branches in the original sampling recipe and Algorithms 3/5; verified that no later acceptance corrects the final duration; checked first-iteration unit importance weights; compared exact EM sufficient statistics and independently simulated the printed law. Re-read the full model/censoring definition and all learning/M-step arguments after constructing the example.

Confidence.

High. The endpoint-conditioned density is exactly uniform while the specified routine samples a nonuniform truncated exponential. All relevant latent states, transitions, censoring and observation conditions are explicit, and the failure persists with a correct forward filter and unlimited Monte Carlo samples.

findings.title: The mixture augmentation does not sample the defined subset posterior
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2018__accepted__v19-17-084-I01 — The mixture augmentation does not sample the defined subset posterior
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** Original PDF page5, Eq.(5); AppendixB, PDF page30, Eqs.(35)–(36), and page31, Eqs.(40)–(41). The same updates underpin the Gaussian-mixture demonstration on PDF page15, Section4.2/Table1, and the probabilistic-parafac demonstration on PDF pages20–21, Section4.4/Figure5/Table6. The referenced June2018 arXiv v4 supplement gives the corresponding Gaussian-mixture updates on page40, Eqs.(57)–(59), and parafac updates on page42, Eqs.(62)–(65).

**Claim.** Eq.(5) defines a subset posterior proportional to the prior times the **observed-data** likelihood raised to gamma, usually the number of subsets. For a mixture this is

\[
 \pi_\gamma(\theta\mid y)\ \propto\ \pi(\theta)
 \prod_i\left\{\sum_h \pi_h f_h(y_i\mid\theta)\right\}^{\gamma}.
\]

AppendixB claims its data-augmentation updates sample that posterior. It multiplies allocated sufficient counts by gamma in the parameter updates, then samples only one ordinary, unpowered allocation per observation in Eq.(41). The finite Gaussian-mixture and parafac studies use the same recipe and are presented as demonstrations of WASP's nonlinear/non-Gaussian applicability and posterior accuracy.

**Error and evidence.** Powering does not commute with integrating a latent allocation. There are two related problems in the same recipe:

1. Its stated full conditionals are incompatible. Holding all component parameters fixed at any finite means and positive variances, let p be the weight of component1 and z one allocation. The parameter conditional implies
   \[
   \frac{q(p\mid z=1,\ldots)}{q(p\mid z=2,\ldots)}
      = C\left\{\frac p{1-p}\right\}^{\gamma}.
   \]
   Any compatible z-conditional must therefore have allocation odds proportional to \(\{p/(1-p)\}^{\gamma}\). Eq.(41) instead uses odds proportional to \(p/(1-p)\). Taking p=.25 and.75 yields a cross-odds ratio \(9^{\gamma}\) from one conditional and9 from the other. For gamma>1 these cannot be the conditionals of one joint distribution. Gaussian densities are strictly positive at these parameter values, so this does not depend on zero-probability components.

2. Merely raising Eq.(41)'s allocation probabilities to gamma would still not give Eq.(5). That would sum \(\{\pi_h f_h(y)\}^{\gamma}\) over a single shared allocation, rather than raise \(\sum_h\pi_h f_h(y)\) to gamma. For integer gamma the latter includes all combinations of **independent replica allocations**.

The following exact check goes beyond conditional incompatibility: a whole sweep changes the intended posterior marginal under the paper's own Gaussian-mixture prior. Use L=2,p=2 as in Section4.2, one observation y=(0,0), gamma=5, and precisely Eq.(17):

\[
 p\sim\operatorname{Beta}(1/2,1/2),\quad
 \Sigma_h\sim\operatorname{IW}_2(2,4I),\quad
 \mu_h\mid\Sigma_h\sim N_2(0,100\Sigma_h),
\]

independently across components. No component parameter is held fixed. Grant standard prior-only draws for an empty component; the error does not depend on an empty empirical mean in the released code.

For a single component density at zero, integrating these priors gives

\[
 M_j=E\{f_h(0)^j\}
   =\frac{j!}{(8\pi)^j(1+100j)}.
\]

Indeed integration over the mean gives \((1+100j)^{-1}\), and the inverse-Wishart determinant moment supplies the remaining factor. Expanding the intended powered marginal and integrating the two component priors shows that its p-marginal is a mixture of

\[
 \operatorname{Beta}(1/2+j,1/2+5-j),\quad j=0,\ldots,5,
\]

with weights proportional to

\[
 \frac{(1/2)_j(1/2)_{5-j}}
 {(1+100j)\{1+100(5-j)\}},
\]

where \((a)_j\) is the rising factorial. All six weights are positive. Exact rational arithmetic gives

\[
 E_{\mathrm{intended}}p^2
 =\frac{179114938415}{412387101528}
 =0.4343369076077627.
\]

Start the printed sampler at this intended posterior, with its ordinary allocation conditional. Exchange symmetry makes its single z equal to either component with probability1/2. Its next weight update uses gamma copies of that **same** allocation, so its p-marginal becomes

\[
 \tfrac12\operatorname{Beta}(5.5,.5)
 +\tfrac12\operatorname{Beta}(.5,5.5),\qquad
 Ep^2=\frac{73}{168}=0.4345238095238095.
\]

The remaining mean, covariance and allocation updates do not change p. The exact positive difference is

\[
 \frac{67441447}{360838713837}>0.
\]

Thus the intended posterior is not invariant under a full parameter sweep. This is a finite sampler counterexample, not a claim that Theorem4's asymptotic assumptions hold for a one-observation mixture. The weight functional is bounded and has finite second moment.

Additional identifiable submodel controls show that the mechanism can materially affect uncertainty. For two known overlapping Bernoulli components with probabilities.8 and.2, prior p~Beta(.5,.5), and a balanced m=100 subset, deterministic integration of the finite latent-count transition kernel gives stationary-to-target variance ratios **2.59699 for gamma5** and **4.58467 for gamma10**. Refinement from256 to512 quadrature nodes agrees below1e-9; transition rows sum to one within1.60e-12; gamma1 recovers the target. These numbers quantify a controlled example and are not claimed to reproduce Table1 or Table6.

The error is present in the authenticated repository cited on original PDF page24, commit `a3f415cfe4276776a5116459d51491620029c357`:

- [mixtures/code/wasp_sampler.R](https://github.com/blayes/WASP/blob/a3f415cfe4276776a5116459d51491620029c357/mixtures/code/wasp_sampler.R), lines32/39–47 multiply component counts by nrep; lines52–57 draw one unpowered allocation.
- [parafac/code/parafac_dx_sub.m](https://github.com/blayes/WASP/blob/a3f415cfe4276776a5116459d51491620029c357/parafac/code/parafac_dx_sub.m), lines90–106 draw one unpowered allocation, while lines118 and127 multiply component/stick counts by nrep.

The complete supplementary derivations reproduce the same mismatch, so an omitted exponent in one printed line does not resolve it.

**Reason for rejection.** General extension of existing samplers and two principal nonlinear/non-Gaussian demonstrations are central contributions. Those demonstrations use sampling procedures that do not target the powered subset posterior defining WASP; consequently their posterior comparisons do not validate the claimed method. This is a demonstrated flaw in the empirical procedure, not a request for more experiments. Repair requires a different sampler for the powered **marginal** likelihood, or independent replica allocations, followed by fresh posterior accuracy and timing comparisons. Changing only the printed allocation exponent is insufficient. The Gaussian linear-model theorem, abstract barycenter construction and correctly marginalized LME sampling are outside this finding; their survival does not supply the missing valid nonlinear/non-Gaussian evidence for the paper as written.

**Discovery method.** Traced Eq.(5)'s observed likelihood through the AppendixB augmentation and noticed that a power had been moved inside a latent-variable calculation while allocations stayed unpowered.

**Verification method.** Rechecked original rendered PDF pages30–31 and the complete supplementary sampler derivations; inspected the exact cited source and experiment entrypoints; derived the positive-density conditional cycle and full-prior marginal non-invariance; computed the rational moments and independent finite transition kernels. Root independently verified the original pages, source lines, cross odds and a simpler exact stationary counterexample. The actual-prior rational check is reproducible with wasp084-exact-published-prior.py; numeric controls with wasp084-controls.py.

**Empirical limits.** Historical full-scale tables were not regenerated. The strongly separated Gaussian-mixture simulation could have a small practical error; no specific printed accuracy is declared numerically false. A native simple one-variable parafac control did not demonstrate a material marginal discrepancy and is retained as a negative control. The source, exact posterior non-invariance and required sampler change establish the finding; missing historical outputs do not.

**Confidence: High.** Exact rational non-invariance uses the paper's stated prior and model; an independent conditional argument and the cited implementation confirm the mechanism. The rejection assessment is scoped to the unsupported central sampler generality and two empirical demonstrations.

findings.title: The claimed matching spectral lower bound is false
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2018__accepted__v19-17-144__I01 — The claimed matching spectral lower bound is false
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF page14, Theorem 17 and Equation (25); its proof on PDF pages38–39, especially the reduction on page39 from an average of task complexities to task 1. The affected contribution is advertised in Section 1.1 on PDF page3 and the tightness comparison immediately after Equation (25) on page14.

**Claim.** For the group-norm class in Equation (16), Theorem 17 asserts a lower bound on its population local Rademacher complexity with a positive absolute constant `c`. It assumes `lambda_t^1 >= 1/(n R_max^2)` for every task, `r >= 1/n`, and `q >= 1`. For `q=2`, its claimed bound is

```text
LRC(F_2, r)^2 >= (c/n) sum_j min(r, R_max^2 lambda_1^j/T).
```

The task distributions may differ. The identical-eigenvalue-tail assumption is introduced after the theorem for the ensuing comparison, not as a theorem premise. The paper uses the lower bound to establish its explicitly claimed contribution that its LRC upper bounds match lower bounds up to constants.

**Error and evidence.** The following family satisfies all of the theorem's stated assumptions while ruling out every positive absolute `c`.

For each integer `T >= 2`, take:

- `n=T`, `q=2`, `R_max=1`, and `r=1/T=1/n`.
- `H=R`, input space `{0,1}`, feature map `phi(x)=x`, and kernel `k(x,x')=xx'`. The kernel bound is `K=1` for every `T`.
- Task1 has `X=1` surely. Each other task has i.i.d. `Bernoulli(1/T)` observations. All observations are independent across tasks as well.

The paper defines its covariance operator as the uncentered second moment `E[phi(X) tensor phi(X)]`. Its only nonzero eigenvalue is therefore `lambda_1^1=1` in task 1 and `lambda_t^1=1/T` in every other task. Every task meets `lambda_t^1 >= 1/(n R_max^2)=1/T`. The operators are trace-class. The class in Equation (16) is the Frobenius ball `sum_t w_t^2 <= 2`, whose functions are uniformly bounded by `sqrt(2)`, independently of `T`. Thus kernel bound, radius, dimension and function envelope all stay fixed in this family.

Let `Z_t=(1/n) sum_i sigma_t^i X_t^i`. Removing the local constraint only enlarges the supremum. The support function of the Frobenius ball and Jensen's inequality give

```text
LRC(F_2,r)
  <= (sqrt(2)/T) E||Z||_2
  <= (sqrt(2)/T) sqrt(sum_t E Z_t^2).
```

Independence and the zero means of the Rademacher signs give `E Z_t^2=lambda_t^1/n`. Hence

```text
LRC(F_2,r)^2
  <= 2/(n T^2) sum_t lambda_t^1
   = 2/(T^3) (1+(T-1)/T)
   = (4-2/T)/T^3.
```

Equation (25), however, uses the task 1 spectrum and would require

```text
LRC(F_2,r)^2 >= (c/T) min(1/T,1/T) = c/T^2.
```

Both inequalities could hold only if `c <= 4/T-2/T^2` for every `T`. The right side tends to zero. For any proposed positive absolute constant, choosing `T>4/c` yields a contradiction. This is an analytic upper-versus-lower contradiction and requires no numerical approximation or empirical rerun.

The unsupported proof step is visible on page39: different task distributions are replaced by the complexity of task 1. A second control shows that adding identical task spectra alone does not repair the entire theorem's radius-general statement. Set `T=n=1`, `R_max=m`, `r=1`, and `X~Bernoulli(1/m^2)` under the same fixed kernel. Then `lambda^1=1/m^2=1/(nR_max^2)`. Localization restricts `|w|<=m`, within the stated norm ball. The exact LRC is `m Pr(X=1)=1/m`, while Equation (25) requires it to be at least `sqrt(c)`. Letting the integer `m` grow again contradicts an absolute positive constant. The cited unit-ball lower bound does not justify discarding the relevant envelope/sampling restrictions when changing the radius.

**Reason for rejection.** Matching lower bounds and tightness are an expressly advertised main theoretical contribution, and Theorem 17 is the result used to establish it. That result is false over its stated heterogeneous-task and radius regimes. No adjustment of a universal numerical constant repairs either family. Establishing an appropriate replacement requires additional distribution/normalization restrictions and a revised scope for the claimed sharpness result, or withdrawal of that contribution. This changes the recommendation from accept to reject for the paper as written.

This finding concerns the promised **LRC matching/tightness contribution**. It does not claim that the generic upper bound, the Talagrand inequality, or every equal-spectrum excess-risk rate is false. As Remark 18 itself explains, LRC tightness is also distinct from optimality of an empirical minimizer's risk.

**Discovery method.** Tracing the lower-bound proof revealed the replacement of an average of potentially different task complexities by task 1 and an unverified radius-scaled application of a single-task spectral lower bound. These suggested testing unequal task covariances and rare nonzero features.

**Verification method.** Read the complete 47-page paper, including all appendices; rechecked the original rendered theorem, definitions, surrounding assumptions and proof pages; derived the fixed-constant family above and the exact one-task control; and checked rational certificates in the reviewer script. Independent bounded review re-read the original contribution/assumption/proof context and independently derived the same fixed-constant contradiction. The primary [Mendelson (2003) paper](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume4/mendelson03a/mendelson03a.pdf), Theorem 2.1 on PDF page7, was checked for the unit-ball lower-bound conditions. The counterexamples are self-contained and do not depend on that citation's interpretation.

**Confidence: High.** Every stated assumption is checked explicitly. The primary counterexample keeps the relevant radius, kernel and envelope constants fixed, and its exact necessary upper bound on `c` tends to zero. The single-task control and independent original-PDF verification provide additional checks. The rejection rationale is confined to the explicitly claimed matching/tightness contribution.
