Its only nonzero eigenvalue is therefore \(\lambda _{1}^{1}=1\) in task 1 and \(\lambda _{t}^{1}=1/T\) in every other task. Every task meets lambda_t^1 >= 1/(n R_max^2)=1/T. The operators are trace-class. The class in Equation (16) is the Frobenius ball \(\sum _{t} w_{t}^{2} \le 2\), whose functions are uniformly bounded by \(\operatorname{sqrt}(2)\), independently of \(T\). Thus kernel bound, radius, dimension and function envelope all stay fixed in this family.

Let \(Z_t=\frac{1}{n}\sum_i\sigma_t^i X_t^i\). Removing the local constraint only enlarges the supremum. The support function of the Frobenius ball and Jensen's inequality give

LRC(F_2,r)
  <= (sqrt(2)/T) E||Z||_2
  <= (sqrt(2)/T) sqrt(sum_t E Z_t^2).

Independence and the zero means of the Rademacher signs give \(E Z_{t}^{2}=\lambda _{t}^{1}/n\). Hence

LRC(F_2,r)^2
  <= 2/(n T^2) sum_t lambda_t^1
   = 2/(T^3) (1+(T-1)/T)
   = (4-2/T)/T^3.

Equation (25), however, uses the task 1 spectrum and would require

LRC(F_2,r)^2 >= (c/T) min(1/T,1/T) = c/T^2.

Both inequalities could hold only if \(c \le 4/T-2/T^{2}\) for every \(T\). The right side tends to zero. For any proposed positive absolute constant, choosing \(T>4/c\) yields a contradiction. This is an analytic upper-versus-lower contradiction and requires no numerical approximation or empirical rerun.

The unsupported proof step is visible on page39: different task distributions are replaced by the complexity of task 1. A second control shows that adding identical task spectra alone does not repair the entire theorem's radius-general statement. Set \(T=n=1\), R_max=m, \(r=1\), and \(X\sim \operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/m^{2})\) under the same fixed kernel. Then lambda^1=1/m^2=1/(nR_max^2). Localization restricts \(|w|\le m\), within the stated norm ball. The exact LRC is \(m \Pr (X=1)=1/m\), while Equation (25) requires it to be at least \(\operatorname{sqrt}(c)\). Letting the integer \(m\) grow again contradicts an absolute positive constant. The cited unit-ball lower bound does not justify discarding the relevant envelope/sampling restrictions when changing the radius.

Reason for rejection.

Matching lower bounds and tightness are an expressly advertised main theoretical contribution, and Theorem 17 is the result used to establish it. That result is false over its stated heterogeneous-task and radius regimes. No adjustment of a universal numerical constant repairs either family. Establishing an appropriate replacement requires additional distribution/normalization restrictions and a revised scope for the claimed sharpness result, or withdrawal of that contribution. This changes the recommendation from accept to reject for the paper as written.

This finding concerns the promised LRC matching/tightness contribution. It does not claim that the generic upper bound, the Talagrand inequality, or every equal-spectrum excess-risk rate is false. As Remark 18 itself explains, LRC tightness is also distinct from optimality of an empirical minimizer's risk.

Discovery method.

Tracing the lower-bound proof revealed the replacement of an average of potentially different task complexities by task 1 and an unverified radius-scaled application of a single-task spectral lower bound. These suggested testing unequal task covariances and rare nonzero features.

Verification method.

Read the complete 47-page paper, including all appendices; rechecked the original rendered theorem, definitions, surrounding assumptions and proof pages; derived the fixed-constant family above and the exact one-task control; and checked rational certificates in the reviewer script. Independent bounded review re-read the original contribution/assumption/proof context and independently derived the same fixed-constant contradiction. The primary Mendelson (2003) paper, Theorem 2.1 on PDF page7, was checked for the unit-ball lower-bound conditions. The counterexamples are self-contained and do not depend on that citation's interpretation.

Confidence: High.

Every stated assumption is checked explicitly. The primary counterexample keeps the relevant radius, kernel and envelope constants fixed, and its exact necessary upper bound on \(c\) tends to zero. The single-task control and independent original-PDF verification provide additional checks. The rejection rationale is confined to the explicitly claimed matching/tightness contribution.

findings.title: Exact nonstationary two-cycle contradicts the general convergence theorem
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2018__accepted__v19-17-244-I01 — Exact nonstationary two-cycle contradicts the general convergence theorem
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF16, Theorem9(ii); PDF10, Algorithm1 Eqs13–15; PDF29, Lemma17(a,c). The supporting variational claim is Definition13/Lemma14 on PDF26–28, with its proof in AppendixB.1–B.2, PDF40–44, and its use in AppendixB.4/C, PDF44–45.

**Claim.** For any linear measurement operator and compatible data, Algorithm1 with 0<p<=1 and positive limiting smoothing parameter has only stationary accumulation points of the smoothed Schatten-p objective, under the measurement constraint (Theorem9(ii)). No null-space-property assumption appears in this part. Lemma17 asserts monotonicity of the corresponding auxiliary objective and vanishing consecutive-iterate differences. The paper derives these from an alternating-minimization interpretation of its harmonic weights.

**Error and evidence.** There is a two-by-two real instance, from the prescribed identity-weight initialization, with an exact permanent two-cycle. Both smoothing parameters remain strictly positive, and one accumulation point has a strictly nonzero feasible directional derivative. The construction below specifies its parameter exactly by a continuous scalar equation with certified opposite endpoint signs; a rounded numerical parameter is not substituted for the exact root.

Let s=1/1000, p=1/2 and the input rank estimate be1. For a real parameter h define

\[
A=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&s\end{pmatrix},\qquad
H_h=\begin{pmatrix}-sh&1\\-1&h\end{pmatrix},
\]

and the surjective linear operator

\[
\Phi_h(X)=(X_{11}+shX_{12},\;X_{21}+X_{12},\;X_{22}-hX_{12}),
\qquad Y=(1,0,s).
\]

Its feasible set is exactly A+tH_h (t real, or complex in the paper's complex domain). Since the Frobenius inner product of A and H_h is -sh+sh=0, the first iterate under the prescribed identity weight is X^(1)=A. Algorithm1 sets epsilon^(1)=min(1,sigma2(A))=s.

At this fixed smoothing value let W_h(t) be the actual harmonic weight of Algorithm1 at X=A+tH_h. Equivalently, put

\[
L(X)=(XX^T+s^2I)^{3/4},\qquad R(X)=(X^TX+s^2I)^{3/4},
\quad W(X)=2[I\otimes L(X)+R(X)\otimes I]^{-1}.
\]

For this real square instance this is exactly Eqs10/15. Write a=vec(A), v=vec(H_h). The unique constrained weighted-least-squares update is the scalar map

\[
f_h(t)=-\frac{v^TW_h(t)a}{v^TW_h(t)v}.
\]

The denominator is positive. All matrices in the fractional powers are positive definite, so this map is continuous in h and t. Define F(h)=f_h(f_h(0)). At zero its inner update has the explicit formula

\[
f_h(0)=\frac{hs(\ell^{-1}-r^{-1})}
{h^2(s^2\ell^{-1}+r^{-1})+4/(\ell+r)},
\qquad \ell=(1+s^2)^{3/4},\quad r=(2s^2)^{3/4}.
\]

The following are outward-rounded interval results at192-bit precision, using closed two-by-two spectral powers and a four-by-four Sylvester matrix inverse:

| Quantity | Certified result |
|---|---|
| F(864/100000) | positive, approximately1.21486242087068e-5 |
| F(865/100000) | negative, approximately-5.90512893293140e-6 |
| f_h(0), throughout this interval | between-.0302 and-.03 |
| sigma2(A+f_h(0)H_h), throughout the interval | greater than.001636, hence greater than s |
| g_s^(1/2)(A) | approximately1.03760628093077 |
| g_s^(1/2)(A+f_h(0)H_h), throughout the interval | greater than1.04427 |
| feasible derivative of g_s^(1/2) at A along H_h | greater than.0812 |

The intermediate value theorem supplies an **exact** h_star in (864/100000,865/100000) with F(h_star)=0. Any such root works. Numerically h_star is approximately.008646726175575702 and t1=f_h_star(0) is approximately-.030075409569939148; these decimals only identify the construction.

Set B=A+t1H_h_star. The strict singular-value inequality above shows the smoothing update at B leaves epsilon=s. The next least-squares update is f_h_star(t1)=F(h_star)=0 and therefore returns A. At A its second singular value is s, so epsilon again remains s. Induction now gives the exact sequence

\[
X^{(1)},X^{(2)},X^{(3)},X^{(4)},\ldots=A,B,A,B,\ldots,
\qquad \epsilon^{(n)}=s>0.
\]

The interval singular-value check can also be reproduced with rational bounds, independently of delicate singular-value subtraction. Uniformly, .03<|t1|<.0302, det(B)>=6555079730639/(4*10^15), and ||B||F<1.001. Thus sigma2(B)=det(B)/sigma1(B)>det(B)/1.001>.001636. These suffice to verify the algorithm's smoothing rule for the whole exact-root bracket.

At the accumulation point A the constrained directional derivative is

\[
\langle\nabla g_s^{1/2}(A),H_{h_\star}\rangle_F
=\tfrac12 h_\star s\big[(2s^2)^{-3/4}-(1+s^2)^{-3/4}\big]>0.
\]

So A is not stationary. This directly falsifies Theorem9(ii), rather than merely identifying a proof gap. The nonzero separation ||B-A||F also falsifies Lemma17(c), and the increase g(B)>g(A), together with the paper's evaluation identity31, falsifies Lemma17(a). All least-squares systems are well-defined because Phi is surjective and W is positive definite. The theorem permits arbitrary compatible Y and does not require a low-rank solution or an NSP in(ii). Even if a rank-one ground truth is desired in its complex domain, a complex root of det(A+tH)=s+h(1-s²)t+(1-sh²)t²=0 gives one with exactly the same Y.

The underlying auxiliary minimization is independently false, even for real full-rank square matrices. Take X=I2, p=1/2, epsilon=10^-4 and

\[
Z=\begin{pmatrix}0&1/3\\10000&0\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Definition13 gives harmonic weights2ab/(a+b) on both diagonal entries of X, for a=1/3,b=10000. Consequently

\[
\mathcal J_{1/2}(I,\epsilon,Z)
=\frac{ab}{a+b}+\frac{\epsilon^2}{4}(a+b)
+\frac34(a^{-1/3}+b^{-1/3})
\approx1.4498463174.
\]

At the claimed Lemma14 minimizer the value is2(1+epsilon²)^(1/4)>2. Thus the supposed minimizer is not a global minimizer. AppendixB.2 contains invalid matrix-power differentiation and orientation deductions; in particular, diagonal BB* does not imply that B is orthonormal or diagonal. The last auxiliary-minimization inequality in AppendixB.4/PDF44 is unsupported and the actual algorithm need not descend. The auxiliary counterexample and cycle concern the same failed variational/convergence argument and are counted as one issue.

**Reason for rejection.** The paper presents a nonconvex optimization method with a general stationary-point convergence guarantee (announced in Section1.1/PDF3 and Section4.1/PDF15), supported by a claimed alternating-minimization framework. That guarantee is false for its exact stated algorithm: it can perpetually cycle through a nonstationary point with positive smoothing, from the prescribed initialization. Correcting a constant, an index or the uniqueness wording does not remove this example. Preserving a general stationary guarantee would require a changed algorithm or additional substantive assumptions and a new convergence argument. This invalidates a central theoretical contribution and warrants rejecting the paper as written. The separate local2-p theorem under a strong NSP (Theorem11) is **not** disproved by this example, and no published recovery-probability figure is alleged numerically false.

**Discovery method.** While tracing the convergence proof into AppendixB, the asserted unique auxiliary minimizer and the inference from diagonal Gram matrices to aligned singular vectors looked unjustified. An off-diagonal full-rank Z then gave a smaller auxiliary value. A targeted affine-line search showed real objective increases, which led to the continuous scalar construction of an exact two-cycle.

**Verification method.** Rechecked Algorithm1, Theorem9(ii), Definition13, Lemmas14/17/18 and AppendicesB/C against the original PDF and inspected full original renders10/16/26/27/28/29/42/43/44/45. The192-bit Arb calculation certifies endpoint signs and uniform bounds; an independent90-digit closed-form SPD-power/Sylvester implementation reproduces them and derives rational determinant/Frobenius bounds for the smoothing check. This is an exact existence argument with certified enclosures, not an extrapolation from a finite floating-point trajectory. Separately, the unchanged released HM implementation reproduces the small published recovery example and16fresh completion fits; these support the scope distinction and do not resolve the theorem failure.

Reproduction artifacts:

- Certified cycle calculation

**Confidence: High.** The counterexample follows the actual algorithm's initialization, unique least-squares steps and adaptive smoothing rule. Opposite endpoint signs, nonzero separation, the smoothing inequality and nonstationarity have independently checked strict margins. The rejection assessment is limited to the false general convergence contribution.

sections.html:
The audit constructs a surjective affine problem for real 2×2 matrices with smoothing parameter 0.001. A parameter h between 0.00864 and 0.00865 makes the update alternate forever between matrices A and B. The objective rises from about 1.037606 at A to more than 1.04427 at B, and the gradient magnitude at A exceeds 0.0812.

\[ A\longmapsto B\longmapsto A,\qquad g(B)>1.04427>1.037606=g(A) \]

findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDFp.9, Definition4; p.18, Section4.3/Equation(11); pp.19–22, Section5 and Figures5–7. The implementation cited on p.19 is GUDHI's Covercomplex module. In its authenticated publication-month source, `GIC.h` at commit`106372ae36905c2892c3dde6b7c36557baf54b34`, lines1111–1158 compute and store extended diagrams, and line1201 sends them to `bottleneck_distance`. The underlying `Persistence_graph.h`, lines88/94, discards every finite point with `death−birth≤epsilon`.

**Claim.** Definition4 requires the bottleneck matching to preserve diagram type and homological dimension. PDFp.8 identifies loops with `Ext−1` and upward branches with `Rel1`, both below the diagonal. Equation(11) defines the bootstrap threshold from this full extended-diagram bottleneck distance. Section5 presents practical confidence calculations for these topological features, including85%regions computed from100bootstrap samples, and identifies GUDHI as the code used.

The paper expressly leaves statistical validity of Mapper bootstrap coverage open on pp.18/22. The error here is that the cited implementation fails to compute even the distance specified in Equation(11).

**Error and evidence.** The released module converts cone-filtration intervals back into original filter coordinates in `compute_PD`, retaining below-diagonal births/deaths. It puts all feature types/dimensions into one `vector<pair<double,double>>`. `compute_distribution` then passes those raw diagrams directly to the ordinary GUDHI bottleneck routine. The latter's constructor keeps a finite point only when

```cpp
std::get<1>(*it) - std::get<0>(*it) > e
```

Consequently every loop and upward-branch point is deleted before any matching. This happens for exact mode`e=0` and the actual default positive tolerance. The routine is entirely insensitive to changes in these feature classes. Pooling the remaining types also violates Definition4; these are manifestations of the same wrong-distance calculation.

An exact countercheck uses these genuine graph signatures:

- A circle with height range`[0,2]`: `Ext0={(0,2)}`, `Ext1={(2,0)}`.
- A monotone interval with the same range: `Ext0={(0,2)}`, `Ext1=empty`.

Their correct typed bottleneck distance is1: match the common trunk at zero cost and send the unmatched loop`(2,0)` to the diagonal, costing`|2−0|/2=1`. An independent reduction over the field with two elements of the finite cone filtration verifies both signatures.

The unchanged original `Persistence_graph.h` and `Internal_point.h` compile in a small C++harness. For the circle/interval pair the constructor deletes`(2,0)`, leaving exactly the same native matching problem as two identical intervals. Its distance is0. An independent exhaustive perfect-matching calculation on that same native graph confirms0 at both tolerances; an above-diagonal-point-versus-empty positive control returns1.

The lost uncertainty can change a bootstrap threshold, rather than merely one pairwise distance. **Exact location.** PDFp.12, Lemma3.2 and Theorem3.3/Equation(14); p.13, dimension-free interpretation and Corollaries3.4/3.5; p.36, AppendixA.2, first inequality in the Rademacher-complexity proof.

**Claim.** For any chosen transportation norm, AssumptionsA/B require only `||(x,y)||≤R` and `sup_{β∈B}||(−β,1)||*=Bbar`. Lemma3.2 claims the loss class has empirical Rademacher complexity at most`2Bbar·R/√N`. Theorem3.3 therefore asserts, for an optimum of the paper's regularizedAD problem(10), with probability at least`1−δ`,

`E|Y−X'βhat| ≤ empirical absolute loss + 2Bbar·R/√N + Bbar·R sqrt(8log(2/δ)/N)`.

The paper explicitly presents this guarantee as independent of dimension.

**Error and evidence.** Bounded individual losses do not justify pulling a common bound through a signed sum and a supremum. Different coordinates of a feasible coefficient can choose which observations incur loss; this destroys the cancellation used on p.36.

An exact counterexample to the lemma takes distinct`x_i=e_i∈R^N`, `y_i=0`, `B=[−1,1]^N`, and joint transportation norm`l1`. Then`R=Bbar=1`, and the loss coordinates`|β_i|` independently range over`[0,1]`. For signs`σ_i`,

`sup_{β∈B}|Σσ_i|β_i|| = max(Nplus,Nminus) = (N+|Σσ_i|)/2`.

Under the paper's own`2/N`normalization the complexity is

`1+E|Σσ_i|/N ≥1`,

whereas its claimed bound tends to0. At`N=16`, the exact complexity is`39203/32768≈1.19638`, exceeding the printed bound`0.5`.

The main theorem itself also fails, for **every optimal solution** on an event with probability exceeding one half:

1. Set`N=400`, `p=160000`. Draw`J`uniformly from`{1,…,p}`, let`X=e_J`, and draw`Y`independently and uniformly from`{−1,1}`. This is a clean iid linear model with true coefficient0 and independent centered noise`Y`.
2. Choose`B=[−1,1]^p`and transportation norm`l1`. AssumptionA holds with`R=2`; AssumptionB holds with`Bbar=1`, because`||(−β,1)||∞=1`for every feasible coefficient. The regularizer in(10) is therefore the constant`epsilon`, for any positive radius.
3. If all training indices`J_i`are distinct, the cube contains an interpolating coefficient`β_{J_i}=Y_i`. Nonnegative empirical loss then implies **every** optimum of(10) has training absolute loss0.
4. For every feasible coefficient, including a data-dependent optimum, a fresh independent response satisfies`E(|Y−β_J||β,J)=1`. Thus the population loss equals1.

The probability of distinct training indices is

`Π_{k=0}^{399}(1−k/160000)=0.6070369452346804`.

The elementary union bound already gives the exact lower certificate

`P(distinct) ≥1−400·399/(2·160000)=401/800=0.50125`.

For`δ=0.1`, the theorem's right side on this event is

`4/√400 + 2sqrt(8log(20)/400) = 0.6895493661361634 <1`.

Consequently Equation(14) fails with probability at least`0.50125`, rather than at most`0.1`. All stated assumptions hold; the true coefficient is feasible. The argument needs neither a selected bad optimizer nor a numerical optimization failure.

**Reason for rejection.** Novel generalization guarantees are a central contribution in the abstract and numbered contribution2on p.5. Theorem3.3, its dimension-free interpretation and sample-size Corollaries3.4/3.5 are false under the stated class. The example's true generalization gap stays1 while the promised bound is below1. A constant or proof-notation correction cannot repair the missing dependence on the actual hypothesis/norm complexity. The claimed general guarantee and its high-dimensional sample-size advice require substantive revision or withdrawal, justifying rejection as written.

**Discovery method.** While tracing Lemma3.2, noticed that the proof bounds a supremum of signed, observation-dependent losses by a bound times the absolute sum of the signs.

**Verification method.** Rechecked the original rendered assumptions/theorem/proof pages; derived an exact binomial Rademacher value; constructed a finite iid model and certified all optima's training loss and exact population loss; computed the distinct-index probability with rational arithmetic and its union lower bound; independently checked a finite interpolation fixture. Bounded original-PDF QA independently checked the argument.

**Confidence: High.** The counterexample meets every theorem premise and violates its stated probability with explicit finite numbers. It does not depend on asymptotic constants, software artifacts or tie-breaking.

findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDFp.17, Lemma3.10, Theorem3.11/Equation(20) and the following claimed`1/N`rate/loss comparison; pp.14–16, Equation(18) and AssumptionsC–G; pp.42–43, AppendixA.11, dual-ball Gaussian-width argument.

**Claim.** The paper bounds the unnormalized absolute-residual sum by`C·mu·Bbar2·w(Bu)`and combines this with the restricted covariance bound to claim an estimation error proportional to

`R·Bbar2·mu·w(Bu)·Psi(β*) / (N·lambda_min)`.

The surrounding text identifies the dual-loss ball with a ball in`R^m`and asserts`1/N`coefficient convergence for absolute loss, faster than the alternatives.

**Error and evidence.** Here`Z`is`m×N`, so`Z'θ`is an`N`-vector. Its dual representation is

`||Z'θ||1 = sup_{v∈[−1,1]^N} θ'Zv`.

The required ball is therefore in`R^N`. Its Gaussian width is exactly

`w([−1,1]^N)=EΣ_{i=1}^N|g_i|=N sqrt(2/pi)`,

and its Euclidean radius is`√N`. That width cancels the`1/N`in Equation(20). Correcting the dimension removes the claimed convergence and the claimed sample-rate advantage of absolute loss. Keeping the printed`R^m`interpretation makes the residual lemma false: bounded centered responses`Y_i=±a/√m`and coefficient0give residual sum`aN/√m`, while the printed fixed-`m`width bound has no`N`growth.

A direct counterexample also refutes the decaying interpretation of Theorem3.11 for the constrained estimator(18), using the **smallest residual budget that admits the true coefficient**.

Let`a=1/4`, `m≥2`, and let`η_1,…,η_m`be independent Rademacher signs. Set

`X_j=aη_j/√m`for`j<m`, `β*=(1/2)e_1`,

`error=aη_m/√m`, `Y=a(η_1/2+η_m)/√m`.

Use the Euclidean transportation norm and the Euclidean unit ball as`B`. The following check the stated assumptions:

- The joint vector is centered and uniformly bounded, with`||(X,Y)||2≤a sqrt(1+5/(4m))<1`; take`R=1`and a valid sub-Gaussian bound`mu=1`.
- `Bbar2=√2`, and`β*∈B`.
- The covariance is`(a²/m)I`except for the`(X_1,Y)`block`(a²/m)[[1,1/2],[1/2,5/4]]`. Its smallest and largest eigenvalues are`(a²/m)(9−√17)/8`and`(a²/m)(9+√17)/8`, respectively. Thus AssumptionG holds with a constant condition number.
- Choose`gamma_N=aN/√m`. This equals the true coefficient's residual sum exactly, so AssumptionE holds with no artificially inflated budget.

At coefficient0the residual sum is

`gamma_N + (a/(2√m)) S_N`, where`S_N=Σ_i η_{i1}η_{im}`.

Therefore0is feasible whenever`S_N≤0`, an event with probability at least`1/2`. On that event it uniquely minimizes the objective`√(1+||β||2²)`in(18). The estimation error is exactly`1/2`.

The restricted-eigenvalue assumption also holds with probability tending to1. Entrywise Hoeffding bounds imply

`P(max_jk |N^−1Σ_i η_ijη_ik−δ_jk|>1/(2m)) ≤2m²exp(−N/(8m²))`.

On the complementary event the covariance inequality holds on the entire unit sphere:`ZZ'≥N·Gamma/2`. Thus AssumptionD holds with`alpha=N·lambda_min/2`, and hence on the paper's descent cone as well.

Take`m=ceil(logN)`. Since`w(A(β*))≤√m`, `mu_bar^4=O(m²)`and the covariance condition number is bounded, the theorem's sample-size condition requires at most`O(m³)`and is satisfied. Both claimed failure terms tend to0: they have the forms`exp(−cN/m²)`and`C4exp(−c'm)`. But the printed`R^m`width gives right side`O(m²/N)→0`, while the actual error is`1/2`with probability at least`1/2−o(1)`. This contradicts that decaying guarantee.

This example directly addresses Equation(18), the estimator specified in Theorem3.11. It does not assert that every constrained budget corresponds to a finite positive penalty in(10). Its budget is the exact true-residual feasibility threshold. Reading`Bu`correctly as`N`-dimensional avoids the dimensional mistake but withdraws the asserted rate instead. The separate missing moment-root notation in the appendix is not used to manufacture a vacuous reading of the intended sub-Gaussian assumptions.

**Reason for rejection.** Coefficient-estimation guarantees and a theoretical explanation for absolute loss's supposed rate advantage are explicitly part of main contribution2on p.5. The dimensional correction destroys the advertised`1/N`guarantee and loss-rate comparison; retaining the decaying interpretation gives an exact counterfamily satisfying all displayed statistical and geometric premises. Repair requires a different estimation analysis and additional substantive conditions or revised claims. This independently warrants rejection as written. The deterministic bound in Theorem3.6, conditional restricted-eigenvalue lemmas and DRO/regularization correspondence are not declared false.

**Discovery method.** While tracing AppendixA.11, noticed that the dual variable has one coordinate per observation, whereas the theorem interpretation uses the data dimension and treats its width as independent of sample size.

**Verification method.** Rechecked original rendered pp.14–17/38–43; derived the cube width exactly; constructed the bounded independent-sign regression model; checked its covariance eigenvalues and norm bounds symbolically; exhaustively checked the minimal-budget event for12signs; verified residual identities and covariance controls at four dimensions; derived an explicit Hoeffding certificate for AssumptionD and the asymptotic contradiction. Bounded independent original-PDF QA checked the contribution scope and counterexample.

**Confidence: High.** The dimension follows directly from matrix multiplication, and the exact width removes the claimed rate. The explicit feasible-estimator family verifies why the decaying interpretation cannot hold, including a nonvacuous confidence and restricted-eigenvalue event.

**Shared reproducible artifacts and limits.** Exact checks and rational fixtures are in unpublished audit files; positive dual/risk controls are in`chen17295-positive-controls.py`. Full-paper notes, `theory-candidates.md`, `targeted-checks.json/.log`, `positive-controls.log`, material-search limits and independent QA are in unpublished audit files. Original2018experiment drivers, seeds and numeric curves were not recovered after repeated primary-source searches; the findings are analytic counterexamples, not claims of rerunning the published simulations or overturning a specific empirical curve.

R·Bbar2·mu·w(Bu)·Psi(β*) / (N·lambda_min).

The surrounding text identifies the dual-loss ball with a ball in\(R^{m}\)and asserts\(\frac{1}{N}\)coefficient convergence for absolute loss, faster than the alternatives.

Here\(Z\)is\(m\times N\), so\(Z^{\prime}\theta\)is an\(N\)-vector. Its dual representation is

\(\lVert Z^{\mathsf{T}}\theta\rVert_1=\sup_{v\in[-1,1]^N}\theta^{\mathsf{T}}Zv\).

The required ball is therefore in\(R^{N}\). Its Gaussian width is exactly

\(w([-1,1]^N)=\mathbb{E}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\lvert g_i\rvert=N\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}\),

and its Euclidean radius is\(\surd N\). That width cancels the\(\frac{1}{N}\)in Equation(20). Correcting the dimension removes the claimed convergence and the claimed sample-rate advantage of absolute loss. Keeping the printed\(R^{m}\)interpretation makes the residual lemma false: bounded centered responses\(Y_{i}=\pm a/\surd m\)and coefficient0give residual sumaN/√m, while the printed fixed-\(m\)width bound has no\(N\)growth.

A direct counterexample also refutes the decaying interpretation of Theorem3.11 for the constrained estimator(18), using the smallest residual budget that admits the true coefficient.

Let\(a=1/4\), \(m\ge 2\), and let\(\eta _{1},\ldots ,\eta _{m}\)be independent Rademacher signs. Set

\(X_{j}=a\eta _{j}/\surd m\)for\(j<m\), \(\beta *=(1/2)e_{1}\),

error=aη_m/√m, \(Y=a(\eta _{1}/2+\eta _{m})/\surd m\).

  • Bbar2=√2, and\(\beta *\in B\).
  • The covariance is\((a^{2}/m)I\)except for the\((X_{1},Y)\)block\((a^{2}/m)[[1,1/2],[1/2,5/4]]\). Its smallest and largest eigenvalues are\((a^{2}/m)(9-\surd 17)/8\)and\((a^{2}/m)(9+\surd 17)/8\), respectively. Thus AssumptionG holds with a constant condition number.

At coefficient0the residual sum is

\(\gamma _{N} + (a/(2\surd m)) S_{N}\), where\(S_N=\sum_i\eta_{i1}\eta_{im}\).

Therefore0is feasible whenever\(S_{N}\le 0\), an event with probability at least\(\frac{1}{2}\). On that event it uniquely minimizes the objective\(\sqrt{1+\lVert\beta\rVert_2^2}\)in(18). The estimation error is exactly\(\frac{1}{2}\).

Coefficient-estimation guarantees and a theoretical explanation for absolute loss's supposed rate advantage are explicitly part of main contribution2on p.5. findings.title: The prescribed component update increases the mixed risk it is claimed to minimize
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2018__accepted__v19-17-402__I01 — The prescribed component update increases the mixed risk it is claimed to minimize
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF pp.6–8, Section2.2, Eq.(7), Eq.(8), Algorithm1 and Lemma2/proof; pp.15–17, Section3.3 and the component-minimization premise of Lemma9. The affected learning claim appears in the abstract/p.1 and introduction/pp.2–3.

**Claim.** The learner fits an intersection of hyperplanes by minimizing the background minimax risk plus the positive hinge risk. Lemma2 says Algorithm1 minimizes the regularized ensemble hinge loss while controlling the background probability. Its proof/p.8 asserts that updating one plane to reduce its hinge loss reduces the ensemble loss whenever that plane has the largest loss and otherwise leaves the ensemble loss unchanged. Section3.3 then uses this same algorithm to minimize each LHM component risk; that component-minimization assertion is a premise of Lemma9's descent proof.

The ensemble loss in Definitions2/4 and Eq.(7) is the sum/average of the **per-example maximum** of the plane hinge losses. Eq.(8) instead minimizes one plane's summed hinge. Reducing the latter does not reduce the former. Re-estimating moments inside other planes also changes a conditional surrogate rather than minimizing the marginal background risk in Eq.(7).

**Error and evidence.** The following specifies an exact counterexample to that update/descent claim. Every covariance used is positive definite, every input and trained weight has norm strictly below one, all single-plane solutions are unique global Eq.(8) minimizers, and there are no sample boundary ties.

Take \(K=2\), \(\gamma=2\), and Eq.(8) regularization \(\lambda=5/8\). The five positive vectors are

\[
(x,1)/4,\qquad x\in\{7/4,-2,-3,3,7/2\}.
\]

For each entry of the multiset

\[
z\in\{-11/10,-1,\underbrace{0,\ldots,0}_{200},1,11/10\},
\]

include the two negative vectors \((z,1\pm1/1000)/4\), giving408 negatives. Their mean is \((0,1/4)\) and covariance is

\[
\operatorname{diag}(13/9600,1/16000000)>0.
\]

Let \(e=10^{-6}\), \(t=1-4e\), and define the following exact algebraic expressions:

\[
c_\pm(\mu,v)=\frac{\mu\pm2\sqrt{tv+e\mu^2}}{t},
\qquad
u(c)=\frac{13/80-c/4}{1+c^2}(1,-c).
\]

Set

\[
\begin{aligned}
c_0&=c_+(0,13/600),\\
c_U&=c_-(21/20,1/400),\\
c_1&=c_+\left(-21/2020,\,221/20200-(21/2020)^2\right).
\end{aligned}
\]

They satisfy \(0<c_1<c_0<c_U<1\). Greedy initialization in Algorithm1 returns

\[
W_0=[4u(c_0),4u(c_U)].
\]

The first plane's positive side selects exactly the four negative vectors corresponding to \(z=1,11/10\). In the unscaled coordinates their first-coordinate mean/variance are \(21/20,1/400\); the second-coordinate mean/variance remain \(1,e\), with zero cross-covariance. The second plane's positive side selects exactly the other404 negatives, whose corresponding first-coordinate mean/variance are \(-21/2020\) and \(221/20200-(21/2020)^2>0\). Therefore the prescribed first refinement returns

\[
W_1=[4u(c_1),4u(c_U)].
\]

These are exact Eq.(8) solutions, not rounded optimizer outputs. To verify them, write the actual weight as \(w=4(a,b)\). This converts the normalized problem to positive coordinates \((x,1)\) with regularization10 and quadratic center \(v_0=(13/80,1/4)\), since all five hinge terms are strictly active. For conditional mean \((\mu,1)\) and covariance \(\operatorname{diag}(v,e)\), the active cone boundary is \(b=-ca\), where \(c=c_+\) for \(a>0\) and \(c=c_-\) for \(a<0\). The expression \(u(c)\) is the Euclidean projection of \(v_0\) onto that boundary. It satisfies the original conic KKT equations with a strictly positive multiplier. Convexity and the positive quadratic regularizer prove unique global optimality. All hinge, sign, conditional-set and covariance inequalities are certified by the accompanying192-bit Arb check. The previous first plane is also **strictly feasible** for the new conditional constraint.

Let \(H(W)=\sum_i\max_j(0,1-w_j^Tx_i)\) and let \(B(W)\) be the paper's marginal moment minimax background risk. Direct evaluation gives:

| Quantity | Greedy \(W_0\) | After prescribed update \(W_1\) |
|---|---:|---:|
| Updated plane's own summed hinge |4.8545361541|4.7539743408|
| Ensemble summed hinge \(H\) |5.6700977945|5.7999251521|
| Marginal background risk \(B\) |0.2000000000|0.3564954764|
| Mixed risk \(B+H/5\) |1.3340195589|1.5164805068|

Both the ensemble hinge and its background risk increase. The sum of squared plane norms also increases, so adding any positive quadratic regularization does not remove this failure; using a summed rather than averaged hinge likewise does not remove it.

The displayed background values are exact intersection risks under the paper's Theorem1, rather than an empirical false-positive fraction or a single-plane upper bound. In the auxiliary coordinates the projection onto the lower boundary also satisfies the upper-plane inequality, and for boundary \(c\) its squared distance is

\[
d^2=\frac{c^2}{13/600+ec^2},\qquad B=(1+d^2)^{-1}.
\]

At \(c=c_0\), \(B=1/5\); at \(c=c_1\), it strictly exceeds0.35649547. After the update, both conditional sets are unchanged. Repeating the same cyclic subproblem updates therefore retains the inferior pair: it is a fixed point with larger stated risk than the feasible greedy initializer.

This establishes failure of the prescribed component update and the published descent/minimization argument. It does not assert a full multi-component LHM cycle or a false uniform generalization bound. Algorithm1 leaves the initial probability/indexing/stopping details unspecified; the finding does not silently repair those details to allege an exact full literal run. Any implementation that performs its prescribed first refinement encounters the certified increase above. Avoiding the refinement does not validate the paper's claimed descent proof for that refinement.

**Reason for rejection.** Mixed-risk minimization by the proposed training algorithms is an explicit central contribution, including the component learner on which the new latent learner relies. The failure occurs in exact global solutions of the stated convex subproblems on normalized, nondegenerate data. The algorithm is optimizing a different conditional, single-plane surrogate, and its claimed monotonic risk reduction does not follow; the advertised component update can increase both terms of the intended objective and settle at a worse feasible model. Consequently, the stated optimization justification for the principal learner and the component-minimization premise of the LHM descent proof are invalid as written.

Repair requires changing the update to optimize the actual per-example maximum/marginal objective, adding an objective-based acceptance mechanism, or withdrawing the claimed risk-minimization/descent guarantee and reassessing the learner as a heuristic. These changes affect the central learning procedure and its claimed guarantee, rather than a constant or an auxiliary proof. The separate uniform risk bounds and particular reported empirical comparisons are not declared false. Under the requested accept-to-reject standard, the central learner's invalid optimization guarantee warrants rejection as written.

**Discovery method.** While tracing Lemma2, noticed that a maximum of summed losses was being used to justify a sum of per-example maxima. Native conic tests then found actual updates that lowered one plane's hinge while raising the ensemble's hinge and marginal background risk.

**Verification method.** Re-read the original definitions, Eq.(8), Algorithms1/2 and Lemmas2/9, inspecting their rendered PDF pages. Constructed the exact normalized dataset above; derived each convex minimizer analytically; certified all KKT, strict hinge, moment, conditional-set, feasibility and risk inequalities with192-bit Arb interval arithmetic. Independently solved82 native SCS updates and retained three additional numerical increases as corroborating controls. An independent bounded audit reconstructed all408 negative vectors, recomputed the4/404 conditional sets and moments, and verified the KKT/strict-feasibility/risk calculations with100-digit arithmetic; its original-PDF check confirms the central claim and the narrow scope.

**Confidence.** High. Exact rational inputs and algebraic minimizers satisfy the original normalization, nonsingularity and conic conditions, with risk increases far from zero. Attribution is limited to the specified update and its optimization guarantee; original figure drivers were unavailable, and no empirical result or full LHM cycle is inferred from this counterexample.

 The helper uses the recorded exact formulas and192-bit Arb arithmetic; it reports every certified claim and numerical enclosure.

findings.title: Gaussian-noise contraction fails under permitted sparse corruption
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2018__accepted__v19-17-473-I01 — Gaussian-noise contraction fails under permitted sparse corruption
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF page11, Theorem5, Eq.(17) and the following noise-ball consequence; PDF pages14–15, Section4.4's claimed improvement over the earlier noise bound; PDF page26, AppendixC. The update is Algorithm1 Option2 (PDF4), equivalently the orthographic formula Eq.(14) (PDF8).

**Claim.** For Y=L*+S*+N*, with independent iid Gaussian N*_ij~N(0,sigma²), row/column corruption fraction at most gamma*, rank r and incoherence mu, assume gamma>10gamma* and (gamma+2gamma*)mu*r<1/64. Theorem5 asserts positive constants C,a,c,eta0 such that, for a positive step eta<eta0, with probability tending1,

\[
 \|L^+-L^*\|_F\le(1-c\eta)\|L-L^*\|_F
 \quad\text{for every }L\in\Gamma,
\]

where Gamma consists of rank-r matrices with error between C*sigma*sqrt((n1+n2)r log(n1n2)) and a*sigma_r(L*). The text deduces convergence into that noise ball and explicitly claims its dimension order is tighter than the prior O(mu²*sqrt(r*n1*n2)*sigma) bound. No lower bound on nonzero corruption magnitudes is assumed.

**Error and evidence.** Take n1=n2=n through multiples of1000. Let J be the all-ones n-by-n matrix and set

\[
 L^*=J,\qquad r=\mu=\sigma=1,\qquad
 \gamma^*=1/1000,\quad\gamma=3/250.

Parent review independently confirmed the original pages, sign and exact identity. Finite simulated examples were retained as controls; they are not asserted to satisfy the unknown-constant annulus or to prove the asymptotic claim by themselves.

**Empirical limits.** The author-linked two-function MATLAB release was recovered and tested. Complete benchmark drivers, seeds, competitor versions, historical Mall matrix/masks and timing outputs were unavailable; historical full-scale plots were not rerun. The paper does not present a separate Gaussian-background experiment validating Theorem5. These limits are recorded separately from the mathematical counterexample.

sections.title: Claim in the paper

sections.title: What may be wrong
sections.html: Moderate positive corruptions can survive trimming and bias the remaining residuals. The resulting update moves away from the true matrix rather than toward it.
sections.markdown: Moderate positive corruptions can survive trimming and bias the remaining residuals. The resulting update moves away from the true matrix rather than toward it.

sections.title: Evidence in brief
sections.html:
Let the true rank-one matrix contain only ones, with unit Gaussian noise. Place corruption of size one on 0.1% of entries in every row and column. Starting just above the true matrix, the retained residual grand mean tends to about −0.00080869. The update subtracts this negative mean, increasing the matrix average and therefore its error for every positive step size.

\[ \operatorname{mean}(L^+)=1+\delta_n-\eta\,\operatorname{mean}(D)>1+\delta_n\qquad(\eta>0,\ \operatorname{mean}(D)<0) \]

findings.title: The central saddle-point guarantee fails because the portfolio objective can be unbounded
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2018__accepted__v19-17-558-I01 — The central saddle-point guarantee fails because the portfolio objective can be unbounded
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF8, Section3.2, Eqs12–13; PDF9–10, Section3.3.1, saddle inequality14 and existence argument19–24. The guarantee is highlighted in the abstract/PDF1, contribution list/PDF3 and conclusion/PDF24; it motivates the solver25–32 and Algorithm1/PDF12. The default parameters are on PDF14.

**Claim.** With positive lambda, gamma and eta, the augmented Lagrangian

\[
L(b,g,\rho)=b^T\phi_t+\frac{\lambda}{2\gamma}\|b-g\|^2
+\lambda\|g\|_1+\frac\eta2(1^Tb-1)^2+\rho(1^Tb-1)
\]

has a finite saddle point satisfying Eq14 for all b,g,rho. The price-derived input is phi_t=-R_t, where R_t=1+1.1log(p_MAX/p_t) and p_MAX is the coordinatewise maximum in the recent window. The paper imposes no upper bound on the spread of R_t and assumes only lambda>0. Existence of this saddle is presented as the significant theoretical improvement that supports its optimization solver.

**Error and evidence.** Both the underlying model12 and L13 can decrease without bound on an exactly self-financing direction. This is an exact counterexample, not just a failure to prove strict convexity.

Take two assets, window length5 and current prices p_t=(1,1). Let an earlier price in that window be (exp(20/11),1), with all other prices in the window equal to(1,1). Every asset price is strictly positive. Eqs10–11 give p_MAX/p_t=(exp(20/11),1), R_t=(3,1) and phi_t=(-3,-1). Use the paper's default lambda=1/2, gamma=1/100 and eta=1/200. For every s>=0 choose

\[
b_s=g_s=(1+s,-s)^T.
\]

Then 1^Tb_s=1 and b_s-g_s=0. Both quadratic penalties and the rho term vanish, for **every** rho. Since ||g_s||_1=1+2s,

\[
L(b_s,g_s,\rho)=-3(1+s)+s+\tfrac12(1+2s)
=-\tfrac52-s\longrightarrow-\infty.
\]

The same expression is the objective of Eq12 on its feasible affine set. For any proposed finite rho_star, Eq14 would require a finite global minimum of L(.,.,rho_star), contradicted by this sequence. Thus the asserted saddle point does not exist under the stated conditions.

Negative entries of b_s are permitted in this optimization stage. Eq12 omits nonnegativity, Eq13 is unconstrained and Eq14 quantifies all b,g,rho. The text on PDF8 and Eqs33/Algorithm1 explicitly apply simplex projection only **after** the iterations to produce an eligible nonnegative portfolio. The final projection therefore does not exclude this counterexample to the preceding saddle theorem. Imposing nonnegativity inside the optimization would change the model and updates; on the simplex, ||b||_1=1 is constant.

More generally, let Delta=max_i R_i-min_i R_i. Choosing b=g=e_i+s(e_i-e_j), with i a maximum-R asset and j a minimum-R asset, gives recession slope 2lambda-Delta. Whenever Delta>2lambda, there is no finite optimum or saddle. This is not repaired by positive gamma/eta or by the positive-definite matrix in Proposition1: that proposition concerns a b-update with **fixed** g, whereas the unbounded direction changes b and g together.

The proof's Huber step is also concretely wrong. Its h(x)=|x|-gamma/2 on |x|>gamma has linear tails and is not strictly convex. At gamma=.01, b=(2,-1), c=(3,-2), H((b+c)/2)=3.99=[H(b)+H(c)]/2, rather than the strict inequality on PDF9. Simply deleting the word “strict” does not fix existence: the unbounded sequence above remains. Slater's condition does not supply a primal optimum for this unbounded problem.

The missing spread condition also fails in recovered benchmark settings, rather than only the constructed example. Using the original official OLPS data matrices and the published w=5,lambda=.5, independent window reconstructions found Delta>1 in2DJIA,7TSE and2NYSE(N) evaluated windows. A reproducible DJIA witness is the update for trading day471 (one-based): current price row470, window rows466–470, maximum-R asset16 and minimum-R asset11. Asset16's last four price relatives are

\[
1.0148478099480327,\quad1.013899049012436,\quad
0.9747474747474747,\quad0.40266469282013323.
\]

Its maximum past-to-current price ratio is the reciprocal of the product of the last two values; asset11's ratio is1. Treating the stored binary floating values as exact rationals, a192-bit outward-rounded logarithm gives

\[
\Delta\in[1.02875072618329657679093635593161462884313665161691560834
\ \mathbin{\pm}\ 2.88\times10^{-57}].
\]

Thus b=g=e16+s(e16-e11) has a strictly negative recession slope less than-.0287. The dataset SHA256 is4e268f3f35ee133680805f972477ac6021f54c58d372eec78b03ffc8dcde718c, from official OLPS Git blob1a14e1b1054b046642ad91ebb6ee1ca410ccc830. The audit retained all exact ratio products and source window indices. These data precede SSPO; a separately pinned historical SSPO dataset version is not provided. As an additional trace check, actual released SSPO code on these five matrices reproduces all five Table3 cumulative wealths to their printed rounding. The exact symbolic counterexample above does not depend on the benchmark-version attribution.

**Reason for rejection.** The paper expressly makes unconditional saddle existence a central theoretical contribution and the foundation of its new solver. Its proposed sparse-portfolio optimization can have no solution, including in recovered default benchmark conditions. This removes that optimization foundation; it is not an incorrect constant or a local proof wording issue. Adding Delta<=2lambda would exclude those evaluated cases, while changing lambda adaptively, adding leverage/nonnegativity constraints or changing the objective would alter the method and require new analysis and evaluation. The reported finite, projected trading heuristic may still produce good returns, but that does not preserve the false central theoretical contribution. This warrants rejection of the paper as written. This finding does **not** claim that finite projected outputs cannot be computed, that Proposition1's individual quadratic minimizer is false, or that the reported wealth numbers are numerically wrong.

**Discovery method.** Tracing the claimed saddle proof revealed that a Huber function with linear tails was called strictly convex. Examining recession directions of the actual linear-plus-l1 objective then showed that its penalty can be dominated by the linear return term on the self-financing subspace.

**Verification method.** Read all28published pages (no appendix) and rechecked the full original renders8–12/14/18, including model domain, price transformation, saddle quantifiers, default parameters and final projection. Verified the symbolic counterexample with exact rational arithmetic; derived the general spread condition. Independently reconstructed actual benchmark windows using cumulative log prices and direct four-return products, then certified the DJIA witness with192-bit Arb intervals. A second reviewer checked original equations, exact recession, benchmark counts and window indexing independently. Recovered the publisher-linked author repository, pinned source upload313cab82653e843d65122de1ee77906249f2860d and verified original Git blob hashes. Native Octave executes the unmodified source, with only the documented Eq32-equivalent wthresh compatibility helper; all five gross wealth results match Table3 rounding. Original proprietary MATLAB timing environment and competitor reruns are not claimed.

Reproduction artifacts:

- Certified original-data witness

**Confidence: High.** The exact admissible positive-price example makes both stabilizing penalties identically zero and proves unboundedness for every dual value. The original PDF explicitly allows the relevant b,g domain before projection. Independent verification and certified benchmark margins corroborate the result; the conclusion is confined to the false central saddle/optimization claim.

findings.title: The general-graph minimax lower bound and the advertised optimality fail on a connected graph
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2018__accepted__v19-17-607-I01 — The general-graph minimax lower bound and the advertised optimality fail on a connected graph
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF p.13, Section 3.2, Theorem 4/Eq. (15) and the surrounding minimax-optimality claims; PDF p.10, prescribed regularization in Eqs. (9)–(10); Appendix B, Lemma 25/Eqs. (105)–(107), PDF p.49, and its proof Eqs. (114), (120)–(121), PDF p.50. PDF pagination and printed pagination agree.

**Claim.** Under the stated independent graph-sampling model, users are uniform, item pairs follow the symmetric probability matrix P, and comparison labels follow the multinomial-logit model. The parameter has entries bounded by alpha and is centered on each connected component. Theorem 4 asserts, for rank r, the following lower bound on expected rescaled Laplacian error:

\[
\inf_{\widehat\Theta}\sup_{\Theta\in\Omega_\alpha,\,\operatorname{rank}\Theta\le r}
\mathbb E\frac{\|(\widehat\Theta-\Theta)L^{1/2}\|_F}{\sqrt{d_1}}
\ge c\min\left\{e^{-\alpha}\sqrt{\frac{rd_1}{n}},
\alpha\max\left[\sqrt{\frac r{\operatorname{tr}(L_r^\dagger)}},
\frac{d_2}{\sqrt{d_1\log d}}\right]\right\}.
\]

The display writes the supremum over Omega with a rank-r premise. The counterexample below is uniform over the entire bounded class, so it applies whether the premise is interpreted as rank at most r or exactly r. The theorem says “a constant c>0”; the claimed scaling and optimality require this constant to be independent of dimension and the chosen graph. Allowing arbitrary graph/dimension dependence would abandon that assertion. The accompanying text claims this establishes sharpness up to logarithms and that no other algorithm can significantly improve on the proposed nuclear-norm estimator.

**Error and evidence: an observable estimator beats the lower bound.** For any integer m>=2 set

\[
d_1=d_2=d=m^4,\quad r=m^2,\quad n=d^2,\quad \alpha=1,\quad\epsilon=d^{-4}.
\]

Let P_edge place probability 1/2 on each ordered pair (1,2) and (2,1), and let P_complete place probability 1/[d(d-1)] on each ordered pair with distinct items. Choose

\[
P=(1-\epsilon)P_{\rm edge}+\epsilon P_{\rm complete},\quad
v=e_1-e_2,\quad H=I-\mathbf1\mathbf1^T/d,
\quad L=\frac{1-\epsilon}{2}vv^T+\frac\epsilon{d-1}H.
\]

P is symmetric, has total mass one, and gives every distinct item pair positive probability. Thus the graph is connected, exactly as allowed by the paper. Its Laplacian has trace one, eigenvalue lambda_h=1-epsilon+epsilon/(d-1) along v, and eigenvalue epsilon/(d-1) on the other d-2 contrast directions. All observations and parameters below satisfy the paper's model and centering convention.

Use only observations of the **observed** unordered pair {1,2}; no latent mixture indicator is available or required. Canonicalize their labels so a success always means item 1 wins. Let N_i be their count for user i, S_i the successes, delta_i=Theta_i1-Theta_i2, and a=1/(1+e^2). Define

\[
\widehat p_i=\operatorname{clip}_{[a,1-a]}\frac{S_i+1/2}{N_i+1},\qquad
\widehat\delta_i=\log\frac{\widehat p_i}{1-\widehat p_i},\qquad
\widehat\Theta_{i,:}=(\widehat\delta_i/2,-\widehat\delta_i/2,0,\ldots,0).
\]

This is a measurable estimator using comparison data only. It is centered, bounded by one, and rank at most one. Put q=1-epsilon+2epsilon/[d(d-1)]. Then N_i has Binomial(n,q/d) law, and conditional on N_i, S_i is Binomial(N_i,p_i), where p_i=sigmoid(delta_i) is in [a,1-a]. The following are exact:

\[
\mathbb E\left[\left(\frac{S_i+1/2}{N_i+1}-p_i\right)^2\middle|N_i\right]
=\frac{N_ip_i(1-p_i)+(1/2-p_i)^2}{(N_i+1)^2}
\le\frac1{4(N_i+1)},
\]
\[
\mathbb E\frac1{N_i+1}
=\frac{1-(1-q/d)^{n+1}}{(n+1)q/d}
\le\frac d{(n+1)q}.
\]

Clipping contracts the error in p, and logit is C-Lipschitz on [a,1-a], with C=2+e^2+e^-2<11. Consequently the strong-edge contribution to expected squared rescaled Laplacian error is at most C^2 d/[8(n+1)]; the factor (1-epsilon)/q is at most one. For the remaining term, both matrices have entries in [-1,1], so

\[
\frac\epsilon{d(d-1)}\|(\widehat\Theta-\Theta)H\|_F^2
\le\frac{4\epsilon d}{d-1}\le8\epsilon.
\]

Jensen's inequality therefore proves, **uniformly over all** Theta in Omega_1,

\[
\mathbb E\frac{\|(\widehat\Theta-\Theta)L^{1/2}\|_F}{\sqrt d}
\le\sqrt{\frac{C^2d}{8(n+1)}+8\epsilon}
<\frac5{\sqrt d}=\frac5{m^2}.
\]

In Theorem 4 the first term is 1/(em). Its second term is at least d/sqrt(d log d)=m^2/sqrt(4 log m), larger than the first. The claimed lower bound is thus c/(em), whereas the proved upper bound is 5/m^2. Choosing m>5e/c contradicts it for every fixed positive c. Here r/d tends to zero and n/(rd log d) tends to infinity: this is a sublinear-rank, large-sample counterexample, rather than just an omitted small-sample cap.

**The prescribed estimator can also fail to converge on this family.** The p.10 tuning uses sigma=1 and

\[
\lambda=8\sqrt2\max\left\{\sqrt{\frac{\log(2d)}n},
\frac{\lambda_{\min}(L)^{-1/2}\log(2d)}n\right\}
\ge8\sqrt2\sqrt{d-1}\log(2d)>1.
\]

With probability q^n>=1-d^-2, every observed pair is {1,2}. On that event the gradient G of the **negative** log likelihood at zero is a v^T, where a_i=(N_i/2-S_i)/n, so ||a||_2<=1/2. The dual of the weighted nuclear norm on centered matrices gives

\[
\|GL^{\dagger/2}\|_{\rm op}\le\tfrac12\sqrt{2/\lambda_h}<1<\lambda.
\]

Convexity and the dual-norm inequality imply that the penalized objective strictly increases from zero for every nonzero centered matrix. Connectedness makes the weighted norm definite on this centered space. Hence the unique Eq. (9) solution is zero on this event, regardless of the labels.

Take the true matrix with every row equal to (1,-1,0,...,0). It has rank one, entries bounded by one, and row sums zero. Its rescaled Laplacian error against zero is sqrt(2 lambda_h). Thus the published theoretical tuning has expected error at least (1-d^-2)sqrt(2 lambda_h), tending to sqrt(2), while the comparison-only estimator just constructed has uniform error O(d^-1/2). This disproves the advertised general-graph optimality for that tuning. It does **not** show that every empirically tuned lambda, every empirical-Laplacian version, or a reported experimental curve fails. Theorem 1's upper inequality is not itself contradicted; its right side can be uninformative on this graph.

**The proof contains a concrete impossible packing, not merely an unfilled argument.** In Eq. (114), for d1=d2=d, the random construction has pairwise expected squared L-distance 2delta^2/d, since tr(L)=1. Eq. (120) only upper-bounds that expectation by 2delta^2, but Eq. (121) applies a lower-tail bound as though 2delta^2 were its mean.

More directly, set d=10000, r=1, delta=1 and L=H/(d-1), a legal uniform complete graph. Lemma 25 requires at least floor(exp(10000/256)) matrices in Omega_alphatilde, alphatilde=8sqrt(2 log d)/d, separated by at least one in L-distance. Yet any two such matrices satisfy

\[
\| (A-B)L^{1/2}\|_F\le2\widetilde\alpha d/\sqrt{d-1}
=16\sqrt{2\log(10000)/9999}<1.
\]

The last strict inequality already follows from log(10000)<10 and 5120<9999. Not even two matrices can have the promised separation. This corroborates the defective lower-bound mechanism. It is part of the same issue, counted once.

**Reason for rejection.** General nonuniform comparison graphs and their graph-dependent statistical optimality are a central advertised advance. The theorem giving the claimed information-theoretic limit is false under its own sampling and parameter assumptions, and the prescribed theoretical estimator is polynomially suboptimal on the same connected family. A constant adjustment, logarithm adjustment, or saturation cap cannot fix this asymptotic discrepancy. Correcting it requires changing the general-graph lower bound, optimality claim and associated tuning analysis, or restricting the graph class. The complete-graph and other choice-model contributions do not remove this central failure. This warrants changing accept to reject for the paper as written.

**Discovery method.** Tracing Theorem 4 into its packing argument exposed the use of an upper bound on a mean as a lower-tail center and a normalization incompatible with tr(L)=1. A graph concentrated on one comparison direction then suggested testing the asserted dimension/rank dependence directly.

**Verification method.** Rechecked the original definitions and assumptions, the rendered theorem and packing pages (13,49,50), and the rendered tuning page (10). Derived the observable estimator and exact binomial identities above, verified all graph/parameter constraints and the KKT argument, and obtained independent bounded checks by a second reviewer. Reproducible scripts are ranking607-counter.py, comparisons607-genton-qa.py and comparisons607-genton-tuning-qa.py under unpublished audit files. All completed with actual exit code zero. Controls include 65 exact rational smoothing-MSE cases, 80 exact reciprocal-binomial identities, explicit Laplacian spectra and fresh estimator simulations; the contradiction itself is analytic and does not rely on simulations. Read and checked the rest of the paper after finding this error.

**Confidence: High.** A uniform constructive risk bound contradicts the claimed minimax rate by a growing factor; a separate exact convex-optimality argument establishes failure of the specified tuning. The finite impossible packing and independent original-PDF rechecks provide additional verification. The scope excludes untested historical empirical implementations.

findings.title: The central weight-information bound is false under its stated moment assumptions
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2018__accepted__v19-17-646__I01 — The central weight-information bound is false under its stated moment assumptions
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF p.13, Section 5, Proposition 5.2; PDF pp.31–32, Proposition C.7 and its proof, especially the final variance/concentration display on p.32. The resulting multilayer bound is Corollary 5.3 on PDF p.14 and Corollary C.8 on p.32. The abstract p.1 and discussion on pp.13–14 and 17–19 identify the weight/representation-information link as a main contribution.

**Claim.** For Z=WX, W=epsilon elementwise-multiplied by a deterministic matrix, epsilon_ij independently log-normal(-alpha/2,alpha), Proposition 5.2 assumes uncorrelated input coordinates and uniformly bounded kurtosis. It asserts

    g(alpha) <= [I(X;Z)+TC(Z)]/dim(Z) <= g(alpha)+c,
    c=O(1/dim(X)) <= 1,
    g(alpha)=-0.5 log(1-exp(-alpha)).

It relates alpha to weight information by alpha=exp(-I(W;D)/dim(W)) and concludes that representation information is tightly controlled by weight information. Corollary 5.3 gives a corresponding weight-only upper bound for multilayer networks with arbitrary nonlinearity.

**Scope checked against the original.** Proposition 5.1 immediately before this result explicitly assumes approximately Gaussian output and conditional-output marginals. Proposition 5.2 and its standalone appendix restatement C.7 state only the moment assumptions above; Corollary 5.3/C.8 also does not state a Gaussian premise. The connecting phrase “with some additional hypotheses” could suggest carrying over the preceding Gaussian approximation. This report does **not** claim that the following input satisfies that approximation, or refute a result expressly restricted to a justified Gaussian approximation. It demonstrates that the stated bounded-kurtosis/uncorrelated or even IID hypotheses do not establish the asserted uniform bound, including at arbitrarily large input dimension. Reading the result as approximate instead leaves its advertised uniform error and multilayer guarantee unjustified without substantial further assumptions.

**Error and evidence.** All logarithms below are natural. Let S be a fair sign, J uniform on {0,1,2,3}, and G standard Gaussian, mutually independent. Set

    X = S exp(20J),  mean weight = 1,
    W = exp(-1/2+G),  Z = WX.

Let W be independent of training data D. Then alpha=1, I(W;D)=0, and alpha=exp(-I(W;D)/dim(W)) holds exactly. The paper's renormalized log-variance proxy is also zero at alpha=1, so no factor-of-two or arbitrary-prior-constant convention is needed. Scalar TC(Z)=0. X has mean zero, finite bounded support and kurtosis

    E[X^4]/E[X^2]^2
      = 4 sum_(j=0)^3 exp(80j) / [sum_(j=0)^3 exp(40j)]^2
      < 4.

Dividing X and Z by sqrt(E[X^2]) additionally gives variance-one inputs with |X|<2, without changing mutual information or kurtosis.

The sign of Z determines S exactly, and

    log|Z|+1/2 = 20J+G.

Rounding this quantity to the nearest 20j recovers J unless |G|>=10. Mills' bound gives

    P(error) <= 2 Phi(-10) <= 2 phi(10)/10 < 1.54*10^-23.

Use the deliberately loose error budget delta=10^-10. Fano's inequality for the eight input symbols gives

    I(X;Z) >= log8 - h(delta) - delta log7
             > 2.079441539082659820,

where h is binary entropy in nats. But the largest upper bound allowed by the proposition is

    g(1)+1 = 1.2293375726935409455.

The certified gap exceeds 0.850103966389118874 nats. This is a strict violation, not a numerical estimate of differential entropy.

There is also an arbitrarily-large-dimension example with no zero weights. Take d IID copies of this X, independent log-normal noises with alpha=1, and one output with deterministic weight row

    (1, exp(-100)/d, ..., exp(-100)/d).

Write Z=epsilon_1 X_1+B. Since E epsilon_j=1 and |X_j|<=exp60, E|B|<=exp(-40). On the event

    |G_1|<=9,
    |B|<=(1-exp(-1))*exp(-9.5),

    exp(-40)/[(1-exp(-1))*exp(-9.5)] + 2 phi(9)/9
      < 8.979*10^-14 < delta.

The problem cannot be fixed by merely increasing the additive constant while keeping the same input conditions. Independently choose a fair sign and set X=S R/sqrt(E R^2). Since E R^2>1/4 and E R^4<=E R^2, these distributions all have mean zero, variance one, |X|<2 and kurtosis<4.     H(X)=log2+h(1/4)+(3/4)log(M-1),
    I(X;Z)>=H(X)-h(delta)-delta log(2M-1),

which grows without bound. Therefore no finite replacement constant depending only on alpha and these same uniform support/kurtosis bounds restores an input-independent information bound.

For the printed multilayer corollary, already take two scalar layers with identity nonlinearity and independent alpha=1 weights.     sum_i w_i^4 E[X_i^2]^2 / (sum_i w_i^2 E[X_i^2])^2 = O(1/d).

sections.html:
Let X have an independent fair sign and four equally likely magnitudes exp(20J), with J from zero to three. Choose an independent lognormal weight W=exp(−1/2+G), where G is standard normal. findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF p.9, Proposition3 and Equation10; p.8 definitions of the retrospective design and weights; AppendixA.2, PDF p.28, its self-normalized confidence proof. The legal algorithm state used below is Algorithm1, PDF p.12, lines8–16 and25–28. Consequences appear in Propositions4/6 (PDF pp.10–11), Lemmas4/5 (PDF pp.30–31), and the regret proofs of Propositions8–10 (PDF pp.31–37).

**Claim.** For iid bounded profile samples with mean mu_i, ||x_i,t||<=L, ||beta||<=S, and conditionally R-sub-Gaussian reward noise, Proposition3 claims that, with probability at least1-delta, simultaneously at all times,

`||beta_hat_(t-1)-beta||_(V_(t-1)) <= sqrt(2 log(det(V_(t-1))^(1/2) det(lambda I)^(-1/2)/delta)) + sqrt(lambda) S`.

Here the regression reuses each arm's *current* empirical profile in every historical reward row. Its weights are `1/R_i,t`, where `R_i,t=sqrt(R^2+L^2 S^2/n_i,t)`, and `V=lambda I+sum_(s<t) xhat_(i_s,t) xhat_(i_s,t)'/R_(i_s,t)`.

**Error and evidence.** The claimed confidence event fails with probability arbitrarily close to1 in a legal selected-arm-only delivery setting, even with R=1, independent bounded samples, and no reward noise.

Choose `d=1`, `K=1000`, `L=S=R=lambda=beta=1`, and `delta=1/20`. Every arm has true profile `mu_i=1/2`. Each delivered profile sample is an independent Bernoulli(1/2) variable in{0,1}, independently across arms and deliveries. Every reward is deterministically1/2. Thus all sample norm and mean assumptions hold, the reward mean equals `mu_i beta`, and the zero reward noise is conditionally1-sub-Gaussian. Use exactly delivery case3 on PDF p.7: at step t>1 only arm `i_(t-1)` delivers a profile sample; no arm delivers before the first decision. The algorithm's forced initialization plays arms1,...,K once.

At decision `t=K+1`, after receiving the last initialized arm's first sample and before choosing again, every arm has one reward and one observed profile: `N_i=n_i=1`. Let m be the number of these K independent profile samples that equal1, so `m~Binomial(1000,1/2)`. Every `R_i,t=sqrt(2)`. Substituting into Equations8–10 and Algorithm1's updates gives exactly

```text
V = 1 + m/sqrt(2),
b = m/(2 sqrt(2)) = (V-1)/2,
beta_hat = (V-1)/(2V),
||beta_hat-beta||_V = (V+1)/(2 sqrt(V)),
claimed alpha = sqrt(log(V)+2 log(20)) + 1.
```

On the event `m>=250`, `V>1+2m/3>144` and `V<=1001`. Consequently the actual error is greater than `sqrt(V)/2>6`. In contrast, `V/delta^2<=400400<(5/2)^16<exp(16)`, so the claimed alpha is less than5. The inequality is therefore false throughout this event. Hoeffding's inequality gives

`P(m>=250) >= 1-exp(-125) > 0.95`.

This is a failure probability greater than0.95, whereas Proposition3 allows at most0.05. The executable certificate also computes the exact binomial tail and checks an independent transcription of the printed initialization updates, producing the same V and b. No optimization ambiguity, subsequent tie-breaking, optional artifact, or approximation is needed.

The defect is the errors-in-variables regression underlying the self-normalized argument. Even when the reward and profile samples are independent, the retrospective residual `mu_i beta-xhat_i,t beta` is correlated with its regressor. Here `E[xhat_i (mu_i-xhat_i)]=-1/4` at the checked state. A marginal centered or sub-Gaussian profile error does not supply the conditionally centered predictable increments required by the invoked self-normalized regression theorem. Repeating a current estimated profile across earlier rewards does not remove that dependence. With K increasing in the same construction, `m/K` tends to1/2, `beta_hat` tends to1/2 although beta=1, the actual V-norm error grows as sqrt(K), and the printed radius grows only as sqrt(log(K)). Multiplying the radius by a universal constant, changing inverse-standard-deviation to inverse-variance weights, or correcting an equation's typography cannot fix this counterexample.

**Reason for rejection.** A central advertised contribution is a new algorithm with proved convergence guarantees for unknown profiles, including selected-arm-only delivery. The counterexample falsifies the confidence ellipsoid that is the main theoretical construction for precisely that setting. Propositions4/6, the optimism used by Lemma5, and the main regret derivations explicitly assume that false event. The published proof therefore does not establish the advertised guarantees. Repair requires a valid analysis of the correlated retrospective profile error and new confidence/regret arguments, rather than a local constant or notation correction. That loss of the central theoretical justification warrants rejection of the paper as written. The counterexample does not by itself prove Proposition9's asymptotic orders false: all means coincide here, so its regret is zero. The empirical utility of the heuristic and the problem formulation are not alleged to be false.

**Discovery method.** While tracing Proposition3 into the optimism and regret proofs, noticed that the design replaces all earlier reward regressors with current empirical profiles, while treating profile-estimation errors as ordinary regression noise.

**Verification method.** Re-read the complete paper and appendices; inspected the original rendered definitions, Proposition3, Algorithm1 and AppendixA.2. Constructed the exact case3 distribution above and verified every stated norm, iid, mean, noise, delivery and initialization assumption. Re-derived V, b, the error and claimed radius; proved the m>=250 separation and its probability analytically; computed an exact binomial tail; ran an independent faithful transcription of the forced initialization; checked true-known-profile positive controls. The original cited self-normalized theorem was checked for its predictability/conditional-noise assumptions. Continued checking all other proofs and empirical protocols after finding the issue.

**Confidence: High.** The contradiction uses exact scalar sufficient statistics and a probability bound many orders beyond the allowed failure. It occurs before any discretionary non-initialization action and under bounded iid profiles with deterministic legal rewards. A second reviewer independently checked the original equations, algorithm state and derivation. The confidence rating concerns the false Proposition3 and its unsupported dependent proofs; it does not assert that every dependent theorem's conclusion is itself false.

 The `case3_confidence_counter`, `Algorithm1_initialization_transcription`, and `positive_controls` entries support this issue. Other private diagnostics in that file are not counted as additional qualifying findings. No original released implementation, original experiment driver, seeds or raw Twitter curves were recovered in the targeted search; no empirical rerun or false plotted comparison is claimed. The counterexample is independent of those artifacts.

sections.html:
In the allowed selected-only setting, use one feature, 1,000 users with Bernoulli(1/2) profiles, true coefficient one, and deterministic rewards one-half. After one observation per user, let m be the count of positive estimated profiles. Whenever m is at least 250, the actual normalized error exceeds six but the confidence radius is below five. This event has probability at least 1−exp(−125).

findings.title: Experimental covariance elimination changes the VAE objective
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2018__accepted__v19-17-704-I01 — Experimental covariance elimination changes the VAE objective
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF page15, Section5.1, Experimental Design item2, final paragraph, which applies the deterministic AE covariance elimination to the stochastic VAE. PDF page16 interprets Figure1 as evidence about VAE smoothing; pages18 and20 inherit that covariance protocol for Table1/Figure2; pages22–23 use the same experiment for Figures3–4; page26, AppendixA/Figure5, inherits the MNIST protocol. Compare the defined decoder and ELBO on PDF2, Eq.(2), the functional dependencies on PDF4, and PDF34, AppendixD.5, Eqs.(58)–(61) and footnote14.

**Claim.** The paper defines a Gaussian decoder (p_	heta(xmid z)) whose covariance (Sigma_x(z;	heta)) is a function of the latent value and shared parameters. Section5.1 first eliminates deterministic-AE decoder variances separately for each example, using

[
 [Sigma_x^{(i)}]_{jj}=(x_j^{(i)}-mu_{xj})^2.
]

It then applies the same procedure to the stochastic VAE, describing this as the infinite-capacity limit for the decoder covariance. The resulting experiments are presented as validation of the canonical VAE's robustness, latent-dimension pruning and covariance-driven smoothing. Page16 expressly attributes the Figure1 advantage to integrating over the encoder covariance.

**Error and evidence.** A stochastic VAE cannot generally eliminate its decoder covariance independently for each observed example and latent draw. That changes a single shared function of (z) into a function of both (z) and the observed reconstruction target. Even an infinite-capacity decoder does not resolve this constraint.

Let (q_i(z)=q_phi(zmid x^{(i)})) and hold the encoder and decoder mean (m(z)) fixed. Omitting common Gaussian constants and the common factor (1/2), the covariance-dependent part of the actual VAE objective is

[
 sum_iint q_i(z)sum_jleft[ rac{(x_j^{(i)}-m_j(z))^2}{v_j(z)}+log v_j(z)
ight],dz.
]

Optimizing one shared variance function gives

[
 v_j^*(z)= rac{sum_iq_i(z)(x_j^{(i)}-m_j(z))^2}{sum_iq_i(z)},
]

clipped at the variance floor if one is imposed. The experiment's per-example substitution instead chooses each residual square separately before summing/integrating. It interchanges minimization with a sum of incompatible individual minima.

A concrete exact example is sufficient. Use two observations (x^{(1)}=1,x^{(2)}=2), standard normal prior, both encoders (q_1=q_2=N(0,1)), and the constant decoder mean (m(z)=0). These are legal Gaussian-VAE components, and both KL terms vanish. Any shared decoder variance has pointwise optimum (v(z)=5/2), giving reconstruction objective

[
 L_{
m shared}=2+2log(5/2)=3.83258146374831ldots.
]

The per-example variances are1 and4, giving

[
 L_{
m plugmbox{-}in}=2+log4=3.38629436111989ldots,
 qquad L_{
m shared}-L_{
m plugmbox{-}in}=log(25/16)>0.
]

There is no shared function (v(z)) that equals1 almost everywhere under (q_1) and4 almost everywhere under (q_2), since both Gaussian densities are strictly positive everywhere. The same obstruction holds for distinct nondegenerate Gaussian encoders: their correct optimum is the weighted expression above, not independent residual squares. A controlled example with (q_1=N(-1,1),q_2=N(1,1)) verifies that the shared optimum varies with (z).

This is a change in optimization geometry, not just an additive objective constant. With the same fixed encoders, allow a constant decoder mean and impose variance floor.001. The proper shared objective prefers mean1.5 to mean1:

[
 L_{
m shared}(1.5)=-0.7725887ldots
   <L_{
m shared}(1)=0.6137056ldots.
]

The sample-conditioned criterion reverses that preference:

[
 L_{
m plugmbox{-}in}(1)=-5.9077553ldots
   <L_{
m plugmbox{-}in}(1.5)=-0.7725887ldots.
]

This is a fixed-encoder conditional example; it does not assert a global optimum over all encoders or reproduce a historical NMSE comparison.

As another check, treating the residual-dependent variance as a Gaussian conditional density would give, away from zero residual,

[
 widetilde p(xmid z)= rac{e^{-1/2}}{sqrt{2pi},|x-m(z)|},
]

which is not normalizable. A variance floor removes the zero-residual singularity but leaves the nonintegrable (1/|x|) tail. This explains why the substitution cannot simply be reinterpreted as the defined Gaussian decoder.

The appendix explicitly confirms the relevant distinction. On PDF34, the same per-example, inside-integral variance optimization is introduced as a **lower bound**, and footnote14 says that it cannot be exactly attained even with an infinite-capacity network because it would require a separate network for each sample. That is legitimate as a proof relaxation. It does not justify treating its optimizer as an implementation of the VAE in the empirical sections.

There is some protocol ambiguity because no final experiment code was recovered: the page15 residual might be evaluated at each sampled latent value or at the posterior-mean reconstruction. The first reading produces the per-example relaxation above. The second is also not valid covariance elimination: an example-specific constant variance would require the **expected** squared reconstruction residual, including propagated encoder uncertainty, rather than just the squared mean residual. For affine means, that expectation includes (WSigma_zW^	op). The constant-mean exact example above works under either reading, so the ambiguity does not resolve the shared-decoder contradiction. The report does not claim to have inspected a missing implementation.

**Reason for rejection.** The nonlinear empirical evidence is central to the paper's claimed extension from tractable affine theory to practical VAE robustness, dimension pruning and smoothing. All of those studies inherit the covariance procedure on page15. Their results therefore do not validate the defined canonical VAE objective or isolate its asserted covariance mechanism. This is a demonstrated experimental-model mismatch, not a request for extra experiments without a specific flaw. Repair requires a proper shared covariance decoder and retraining the central comparisons, or explicitly changing the model and withdrawing the claimed empirical validation of canonical-VAE behavior. Approximate separation of encoders near a final deterministic limit does not establish equivalence during training, particularly in the large-variance regions where smoothing is the proposed explanation. The affine PPCA/pruning analysis and legitimate use of a lower bound in proofs are not refuted by this issue.

**Discovery method.** Traced the experimental covariance elimination back to the decoder's functional dependence in Eq.(2), then noticed that AppendixD correctly labels the same operation an unattainable relaxation.

**Verification method.** Read all42 pages and appendices; rechecked rendered original pages2/15/16/18/20/26/34. Derived the shared optimum, the exact overlap contradiction and objective gap, and the density non-normalization. High-precision independent calculations and a separate root review agree. The latter also verified the conditional preference reversal. Continued checking all theoretical and empirical claims; preserving corrections to PPCA normalization and finite-variance exactness are retained separately in the whole-paper notes.

**Empirical limits.** No final authored training code, seeds, numerical outputs, trained weights or original synthetic matrices/masks were recovered in the bounded primary-source search. Historical full-scale experiments were not rerun. No specific printed NMSE, exact trained implementation or corrected historical ranking is declared numerically false; the evidence is the published procedure's incompatibility with its claimed model.

**Confidence: High.** The strict analytic gap and shared-function impossibility satisfy the defined Gaussian model, and the original appendix independently acknowledges precisely this limitation. The rejection consequence is scoped to the central empirical attribution.
